title: Donald Trump Jr. Privately Breaks With His Father On Foreign Policy: Report
desc:
Donald Trump Jr. Privately Breaks With His Father On Foreign Policy: Report

Donald Trump Jr. has privately opposed his father's war with Iran from the very beginning, even personally confronting President Donald Trump with his objections, according to The Atlantic.

The president's eldest son has repeatedly voiced his opposition to the nearly eight-month conflict behind closed doors, despite carefully avoiding any public criticism of his father.

Two anonymous sources who reportedly spoke directly with Trump Jr. said the MAGA leader has repeatedly questioned the military campaign, a position in line with his longstanding opposition to U.S. involvement in foreign wars.

The disagreement reportedly dates back to the beginning of the conflict, when Trump Jr. made his objections known directly to the president.

"Don has kept his views on the subject private, as he would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this, but I can't imagine anyone who knows Don would be surprised by his personal views on the subject," a person supposedly close to Trump Jr. told the leftwing magazine.

Trump Jr. has repeatedly championed his father as a leader who would keep America out of costly foreign entanglements, particularly in the Middle East.

Trump Jr.'s reported opposition also reflects broader divisions within the MAGA movement, where prominent conservative voices have questioned whether the conflict is consistent with the president's campaign promises.

Meanwhile, the war has become an increasingly difficult political issue for Republicans ahead of November's midterm elections.

Rising gasoline prices and mounting economic pressures have fueled public frustration, while a Pew Research Center poll found that 65% of Americans disapprove of the administration's handling of the conflict.

A spokesman for Trump Jr. refused to comment on the report.

title: Hochul Weighs Ending $500 Million Medicaid Adult Day Care Program After Fraud Raids
desc:
Hochul Weighs Ending $500 Million Medicaid Adult Day Care Program After Fraud Raids

Authored by Chase Smith via The Epoch Times,

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has directed the state Department of Health to consider ending the state's Medicaid social adult day care benefit.

The directive came on the same day that state and federal investigators carried out a crackdown on providers suspected of fraud, and on the same day that Hochul announced 16 arrests in a separate auto insurance fraud investigation.

Hochul, a Democrat, stated at an Oct. 20 press conference that she had told the department to look at "all options to eliminate continued fraud, waste and abuse." Those options include phasing out the benefit and moving participants to other services for older New Yorkers. The department's recommendations are due by Dec. 31.

Social adult day care is a non-medical benefit offered through New York's Medicaid managed long-term care program.

It provides daytime supervision, meals, social activities, and personal care in a community setting. More than 400 programs serve about 45,000 Medicaid members at an estimated cost of more than $500 million a year, according to the governor's office. The federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) approves the benefit and helps fund it.

The announcement followed what the governor's office called a months-long investigation targeting more than 100 providers. The state Department of Health, the state Office of the Medicaid Inspector General, and the state attorney general's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit worked with the FBI and the federal Health and Human Services inspector general.

FBI agents and state officials raided programs across New York City on Oct. 20. CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz called the operation the largest enforcement action of its kind.

Hochul said she had gone to Washington to meet with Oz to discuss working together against Medicaid fraud, and that the investigation is targeting providers suspected of money laundering, kickbacks, and improper billing.

"We will find you, we will prosecute you, and we will hold you accountable," Hochul said.

At the same press conference, Hochul announced that a joint investigation by the State Police and the Department of Financial Services had led to 16 arrests in auto insurance fraud cases.

The cases involved nearly $500,000 in attempted fraudulent claims in New York City and Suffolk, Onondaga, Monroe, and Erie counties. Hochul said New Yorkers pay about $4,000 a year for auto insurance, almost $1,500 more than the national average, and that she expects the arrests and insurance reforms in this year's state budget to start lowering rates.

Reviewing Adult Day Care Claims

Regarding the crackdown on adult day care fraud, Hochul ordered the department and the state Medicaid inspector general to require health plans to review social adult day care claims before paying them and to pursue payment suspensions. A moratorium on new providers that the department imposed in July remains in effect until January 2027 and may be extended.

State Health Commissioner Dr. James McDonald said the department will advise Hochul on whether further reforms can deliver accountability or whether participants would do better under other services.

"Medicaid is a lifeline for millions of New Yorkers," Hochul said in a statement. "Protecting that lifeline means defending access to care and defending the integrity of the programs that provide it."

The program has drawn scrutiny before. A February audit by state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli found that managed care plans paid $2.4 billion for adult day care services from January 2019 through October 2024. Payments rose more than 141 percent from 2021 to 2023.

Auditors identified $285 million in questionable payments to centers for dates after at least one plan had dropped them from its network. That included more than $28.6 million to centers terminated for cause, such as fraud.

In one case, a center that one plan cut for fraud, waste, and abuse in 2021 stayed in the networks of 18 other plans and was paid more than $12.9 million afterward.

Auditors also found that a Flushing center with a legal capacity of 323 billed for 530 people on a single day in September 2022.

In its response to the audit, the Health Department said the comptroller's sampling method could overstate how widespread the problems were. The comptroller's office called that statement misleading.

Earlier this year, two people in Brooklyn pleaded guilty to a $68 million adult day care fraud scheme, according to the governor's office.

Asked whether ending the benefit would require federal approval and what services the participants would move to, the state Health Department referred The Epoch Times to the governor's announcement.

Hochul faces Republican Bruce Blakeman in the Nov. 3 governor's race.

Blakeman's campaign and CMS did not respond to a request for comment from The Epoch Times before publication.

title: What Could Democrats Do If They Win The Midterms?
desc:
What Could Democrats Do If They Win The Midterms?

Authored by Nathan Worcester via The Epoch Times,

Even as Republican campaign spending intensifies and the president holds rallies across the country for candidates, many forecasts still look grim for the party in power.

Observers from across the political spectrum predict that Democrats will retake the House, and maybe even the Senate.

What's on the agenda if Democrats win big?

Lawmakers and insiders have outlined a range of possibilities and priorities, including pushback against the Iran war, renewed attention to data centers and artificial intelligence (AI), and congressional investigations targeting everything from the Trump family's finances to the Epstein files.

Yet, President Donald Trump's vetoes may limit Democrats' effectiveness in implementing an affordability-focused plan touted by House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), as could disputes within that party.

Still, some potential outcomes, such as even more delays or blocks of Trump's judicial and Cabinet nominees, seem baked into the cake - especially so if Democrats capture enough seats to bypass tie-breaking votes from Vice President JD Vance.

Pollsters Rich Baris and Mark Mitchell, both of whom predicted Trump's 2024 victory, see Republicans on track to lose the House and possibly the Senate.

During a Sept. 30 press conference, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said that his party was working to take the Senate in part to stymie the president's nominees for the Supreme Court and other courts.

Other possibilities - for instance, another Trump impeachment or two downstream of anticipated investigations - are far short of inevitable, at least partly because of the costs they may impose on some Democrats.

Impeachments

One man who understands the costs of an impeachment proceeding is Joe Cunningham.

The South Carolina Democrat entered the House after an upset victory in 2018, flipping a longstanding Republican district during a midterm election cycle that saw Democrats pick up dozens of seats in the lower chamber.

The lawmaker, who was a member of the moderate Blue Dog Democrats, lost his 2020 reelection bid to the current representative, Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.).

"I could argue that I lost my seat because of my impeachment vote," Cunningham told The Epoch Times, adding, "I don't have any regrets at all."

Rep. Joe Cunningham addresses the crowd at the South Carolina Democratic Party State Convention in Columbia on June 22, 2019. Sean Rayford/Getty Images

Retreading that familiar territory could hurt Democratic incumbents in purple districts, he said, arguing that Democrats should prioritize economic issues rather than an impeachment proceeding he predicted would "consume all the oxygen."

A Senate conviction - the step after impeachment that would actually remove Trump from office - would need support from two-thirds of that chamber. That's hard to imagine in even the rosiest midterm scenarios for Democrats.

Jeffries, though a vocal Trump critic who has accused him of unprecedented corruption, has not committed to impeaching the president.

President Donald Trump takes the stage during a rally at the Majestic Valley Arena in Kalispell, Mont., on Oct. 14, 2026. Travis Gillmore/The Epoch Times

Of course, Trump is not the only administration official Democrats might try to impeach.

Since the second Trump administration began, House Democrats have taken initial steps to oust Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, and Education Secretary Linda McMahon.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has also faced heavy scrutiny from congressional Democrats, who opposed his nomination.

He's also encountered criticism from his own party, including from Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) who accused Blanche of failing to comply with his legislation demanding the release of the Epstein files. A cosponsor of that bill, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), floated impeachment of Blanche in September.

That month, Massie also introduced articles of impeachment against Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, alleging his conduct of the Iran War has violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973. An early House recess short-circuited a push for a vote before the midterms.

Lindsey Cormack, a political scientist at the Stevens Institute of Technology noted Khanna's support for the Hegseth impeachment in an interview with The Epoch Times, saying he "will likely be targeted."

War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks at Anduril Industries in Sparrow Point, Md., on Oct. 6, 2026. Madalina Kilroy/The Epoch Times

Investigations

The bigger - and broader - story might be investigations.

A flurry of subpoenas could hit those in and around the administration as Democrats seek to highlight alleged corruption.

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) have previewed possible probes into 1789 Capital, Donald Trump Jr.'s venture capital firm, and cryptocurrency deals involving the president and his family.

Despite the passage of the Epstein Transparency Act in 2025, redactions in them have driven controversy and could also spur action.

Khanna has said his fellow Democrats should make the Epstein files a major focus in the event they regain control of Congress.

The Justice Department has said the redactions in the files are intended to protect Epstein victims and their families.

Dave Spencer, host of the Practically Political podcast, advised Democrats to pick their battles carefully.

"If they launch too many investigations at once, the American people could begin to see it as overkill," he told The Epoch Times.

Data Centers and AI

Democrats may tackle two closely related issues currently in the spotlight - data centers and AI.

The proliferation of data centers, closely linked to the AI boom and backed by the president, has faced pushback in some local communities.

The Republican-backed Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation aimed at constraining the higher electric bills that hit some consumers after data centers arrive, passed the House but failed in the Senate before that chamber recessed.

Demonstrators protest construction of the Stratos data center in Utah's Box Elder County during a rally at the state Capitol in Salt Lake City on May 23, 2026. Natalie Behring/Getty Images

Democrats have touted a different data center bill, the GRID Savings Act, that would make the companies building out data centers pay for grid and transmission upgrades associated with the boom. GRID stands for Guarding Ratepayers from Increased Demand-costs.

Adam Swart of Crowds on Demand, a paid protester firm, weighed in on grassroots opposition to the buildout to data centers, describing it as "one of the strangest emerging bipartisan issues."

"Tucker Carlson-style Republicans and progressive Democrats increasingly oppose them, while the establishments of both parties largely support them. I suspect Congress eventually passes 'reform' that sounds restrictive but actually makes it easier for the industry to build," he told The Epoch Times.

AI could also spur action.

Amid the tech competition with China and AI-driven economic growth, Trump has cautioned against excessive regulation of the technology, which he has dubbed "super intelligence." Yet some lawmakers, including many Democrats, want more guardrails on those systems as some industry leaders publicly worry about AI safety.

Cunningham said that while he is not in line with the leftmost wing of the Democrats, AI regulation would be "more populist than socialist," and important for his party to address to win back support for 2028.

On Oct. 7, Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), who has worked with Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) on legislation to regulate AI, published a draft version of a bill that would impose a stricter liability standard on AI developers.

Other Priorities

Carmack, the political scientist at the Stevens Institute of Technology, told The Epoch Times she expects Democrats to apply pressure on AI and another contentious matter - immigration - through both legislation and spending negotiations.

Spencer too expects immigration to fuel spending battles between Republicans and Democrats.

Reconciliation bills passed by the GOP-controlled Congress have locked in years of funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement as well as U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

If Democrats perform well enough in the midterms, they could also step up their challenges to tariffs, food stamp cuts, the scope of military spending, and the Iran War, among other Trump policies.

Iranian-made Zolfaghar missiles are displayed at Azadi Square in Tehran on Aug. 2, 2026. Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images

The expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA), or Obamacare, premium subsidies, which triggered the longest government shutdown in history in late 2025, may come back into focus too.

Jeffries and Schumer have both vowed to tackle ACA restrictions championed by Republicans.

Legislation unveiled on Oct. 1 by the New York Democratic delegation, which includes both legislators, would roll back limits to the scope of those who can use ACA premium tax credits, a result of last year's One Big, Beautiful Bill Act.

"The ACA subsidies are a hugely popular issue, and Democrats would almost certainly make restoring them a priority," said Spencer.

Limits and Division

Insiders and experts see a narrow and highly political path to some action as the threat of a Trump veto looms over possible Democratic attempts to legislate on their affordability promises.

Spencer said Democrats could "advance popular legislation that would require Trump to either sign it or veto it."

Cunningham said Democrats could force hard choices through bills targeting the costs of everyday goods. He hopes the party will pursue legislation on prescription drug prices and anti-competitive practices by large corporations.

If Democrats rule Capitol Hill, they will still have to manage conflicts in their own camp.

At the Democratic National Committee's August meeting, dueling resolutions on Immigration and Customs Enforcement - one calling for reform, the other for abolition - underscored ideological divides within the party.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) at a hearing on Capitol Hill on March 5, 2025. Madalina Vasiliu/The Epoch Times

Republican control of Congress during the first half of Trump's second term was marked by conflict, both between different wings of the party and between the House and Senate.

Whether Democrats curb their infighting or not, the future looks explosive.

"This will be an adversarial two years in the run-up to the 2028 presidential elections," Cormack predicted.

Democratic dominance on Capitol Hill - and just how adroitly they tangle with Trump - would also give voters a yardstick ahead of 2028.

"If Democrats want to build a lasting majority - if they want to build some momentum going into 2028 - they've got to start making deliveries for people, for Americans who are getting crushed under this economy," said Cunningham.

title: Watch: Trump Indicates He Doesn't Yet View JD Vance As His Successor
desc:
Watch: Trump Indicates He Doesn't Yet View JD Vance As His Successor

This was awkward and unexpected, but on Tuesday in front of reporters' cameras, President Trump refused to commit to endorsing Vice President JD Vance for president in 2028.

He shrugged off a direct question about it, saying instead that Republicans first need to get through the midterms. Vance, standing behind the president in the Oval, seemed deeply uncomfortable when Trump noted that the two had never discussed such an endorsement - though he did call Vance "deeply talented".

“He’s a very talented person and he’s a very good person,” Trump said when asked alongside Vance in the Oval Office.

“I don’t think we’ve ever talked about it,” the president said, turning to Vance.

“No, sir. I said that too,” Vance chimed in. “Who would believe that?” Trump said, “I don’t talk about it with him. He doesn’t talk about it [with me]. It’s early.”

“We have to get through the midterms. We’ll see how it goes,” he added

Trump insisted it's too early, but the exchange raises huge questions about the Republican Party's future leadership, given other big contenders could be waiting in the wings, like Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The moment was all the more awkward for Vance given it came a mere day after the Vice President said he believed Trump would indeed endorse him if he ran for 2028.

Here's what Vance said in an interview on Monday, though he was obviously speculating:

“I think I would get his endorsement, but I also think there’s something to be said for people actually running their own race,” the vice president said.

“And because the president’s endorsement is so dispositive, you could absolutely see a scenario where the president says, ‘You know what? We need to let like this race play out and not preemptively prejudge the results.’”

JD Vance: I think if I run, Trump will endorse me. I think I would get an endorsement https://t.co/G1obOG43hF

— Headquarters (@HQNewsNow) October 20, 2026

When it comes to one of the biggest Trump policies which has divided the American public - the Iran war and fallout in energy prices - Vance has by and large tried to stay in the background.

And...

Shots fired! JD is still the polling frontrunner and, ignoring an outsider, probably the only one with a path to winning. But Trump is surrounded by people who want other candidates.

— Mark Mitchell, Honest Pollster (@honestpollster) October 21, 2026

Recent public statements issued by Vance in a town hall suggested that he had not been on board the White House's decision to launch the Iran war to begin with. He faced very tough questions particularly on Trump's launching Operation Epic Fury just days ago.

* * *

Meanwhile, speaking of endorsements or lack thereof on other fronts...

JD Vance didn't "go out of his way" to refuse to endorse Netanyahu. He was explicitly asked in an interview and said: I endorse American candidates, not foreign ones. But the fact that Fox News think it's "anti-Israel" to refrain from endorsing Netanyahu -- as if that's a duty of an American Vice President -- shows the subliminal servitude to Israel embedded in the brains for decades of our bipartisan political and media class.

— Glenn Greenwald (@ggreenwald) October 20, 2026

title: Elon Musk Reveals Shocking Details About Migrant Austin Shooter
desc:
Elon Musk Reveals Shocking Details About Migrant Austin Shooter

Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity.news,

Elon Musk has confirmed that Ndiaga Diagne, the 53-year-old Senegal-born naturalized citizen who opened fire outside a downtown Austin bar in March and killed three people, was a former Tesla employee at the company's Gigafactory Texas.

Diagne was fired after he violently assaulted a female coworker who accidentally stepped on his prayer rug during a company-sanctioned break.

Months later he carried out the attack while wearing a "Property of Allah" hoodie and an Iranian-flag shirt.

HOLY SH*T Elon Musk reveals that Ndiaga Diagne, the Muslim man who k*lled 3 people in Austin, was an ex-Tesla employee whom he fired. Diagne was fired after he assaulted a woman for stepping on his prayer rug. Months later, he carried out the shooting. https://t.co/cvqU6KyEly

— Libs of TikTok (@libsoftiktok) October 20, 2026

On March 1, 2026, shortly before 2 a.m., Diagne drove a black Cadillac SUV past Buford's Backyard Beer Garden on West Sixth Street, a popular nightlife strip near the University of Texas. He activated his hazard lights, rolled down the window, and fired a handgun into the patio and sidewalk crowd.

He then parked, exited with an AR-style rifle, and continued shooting along the street before Austin police arrived within roughly a minute and fatally shot him.

Three people were killed: 19-year-old former Texas Tech student Ryder Harrington, 21-year-old University of Texas student Savitha Shanmugasundaram, and 30-year-old Jorge Pederson. Roughly 15 others were wounded.

Diagne, a Pflugerville resident, entered the United States in 2000 on a tourist visa, obtained a green card in 2006 after marrying a U.S. citizen, and was naturalized in 2013.

He had a prior criminal record that included a 2022 hit-and-run reduced to a misdemeanor and later dismissed after probation, as well as domestic violence allegations.

He legally purchased the firearms used in the attack in San Antonio in 2017. A Quran was found in his SUV. The FBI later determined he acted alone with no evidence of direction, funding, or support from a foreign terrorist organization, though investigators noted indicators potentially tied to the conflict involving Iran and Diagne's admiration for Iran's former leadership. He had not previously been on the FBI's radar.

It was this guy. Then the Legacy Media wanted to hide this photo and his motive. https://t.co/PJG6HowzJt

— C3 (@C_3C_3) October 20, 2026

In a recent interview with biographer Walter Isaacson on The Builders, Musk recounted the earlier incident at the factory. "We had someone who was working at the Tesla factory in Austin until December of last year. He was fired because he assaulted a woman who stepped on his prayer rug in the factory," Musk said.

He continued, "She wasn't expecting anyone to be praying in the factory, and he was praying in the factory. She accidentally stepped on his prayer rug, and he assaulted her, violently assaulted her. So he was fired for that. And then a few months later, he went and killed three students in the bar in downtown Austin."

After a long pause, Musk urged "Now, I think we shouldn't let people like that into the country."

Full interview:

A civil lawsuit filed by 65-year-old Tesla employee Lillian Brady in Travis County alleges that on December 4, 2025, Diagne grabbed her and threw her to the ground without provocation while he was praying on a walking path in a common area.

Brady reported the assault to Tesla and local authorities but says the company withheld Diagne's identity, preventing her from pursuing charges. She only connected him to the shooting when she recognized his face in news coverage.

Her attorney, Bob Hilliard, stated: "We already know the shooter violently assaulted a Tesla employee months before the Sixth Street shooting and Tesla had the shooter's name and information about that earlier attack - why they chose not to act or warn law enforcement raises very serious questions the public deserves an answer to."

Brady herself said Tesla's handling was "unethical" and that identifying him earlier "maybe all this could have been avoided."

Tesla has not publicly confirmed the employment details, and some aspects of the assault claim remain allegations in civil court. The company later obtained arbitration for the suit, avoiding a public trial. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said her department had no prior contact with Diagne.

The case illustrates the gap between private employers spotting clear warning signs of violence tied to religious intolerance and an immigration system that naturalized Diagne years earlier with no subsequent removal pathway.

Musk's point is straightforward: screening for individuals who respond to accidental contact with a prayer rug by violently assaulting a coworker is not bigotry; it is basic risk assessment.

The same man later killed three Americans on a night out. Legacy coverage initially emphasized mental health or the broader Iran conflict while downplaying the "Property of Allah" clothing and the prior workplace assault. The photo of Diagne in the hoodie circulated widely on social media once available.

Diagne's history of family violence allegations, the hit-and-run, and the factory incident were not secret. Yet he remained in the country, obtained firearms legally, and was able to work at a major American manufacturer until the prayer-rug assault forced his termination.

The FBI's conclusion that he acted alone does not erase the pattern or the preventable nature of the earlier violence. Screening for ideological incompatibility with the rule of law and equal treatment of women is not optional when the alternative is more dead Americans on Sixth Street.

title: Situational Unawareness: Banks Ran Out Of Room To Lever Up The AI Trade, So They Made More
desc:
Situational Unawareness: Banks Ran Out Of Room To Lever Up The AI Trade, So They Made More

When a bank runs out of room to lend to hedge funds piling into the most crowded trade on the planet, there are two options: stop lending, or find more room. Barclays found more room...

According to a Bloomberg exclusive published Tuesday, Barclays (BARC) executives wanted extra capacity to lend more aggressively to hedge fund clients as Asian AI stocks went vertical earlier this year. The fix: the bank's macro rates traders ended up lending part of their own capital allocation to the prime financing business through an internal auction. The reason they had to: over the summer Barclays had reached its maximum limits on how much financing it could extend to hedge fund clients in Asia. Bloomberg's verdict: Barclays and its peers are "finding ways to meet demand, despite bumping up against internal constraints."

In other words, the internal risk limits did their job, flagged that the bank had lent enough... and the bank responded by moving the goalposts.

Below we walk through why this matters, why Barclays is hardly alone, and why Goldman's own prime book data shows exactly how the banks "fixed" the problem (hint: more shorts, not fewer longs).

"Disciplined"... Right Up To The Limit

The pitch inside Barclays, per Bloomberg's sources, was simple: allocate more balance sheet to higher-returning businesses like prime brokerage (housed in the global markets unit run by Adeel Khan) given the "huge growth" expected in Asian tech stocks. Rates traders, whose returns on balance sheet don't look nearly as sexy as financing Korean memory stocks at peak euphoria, became the donors.

Barclays' official line:

"We deploy our investment bank balance sheet dynamically, responding to client opportunities while maintaining a disciplined approach to risk and returns."

Translation: we found a client opportunity, and we deployed dynamically. Meanwhile, the "disciplined" part kicked in only after the limit was hit.

Regular readers will recall that the Bank of England had already started poking around exactly this corner of the market just as the AI trade was cracking in July:

Bank of England probes Asian equity risk at prime brokers

Korean degens about to blow up the world

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) July 29, 2026

And as we noted when regulators finally found their situational awareness (Sep 24), the BoE is specifically looking at the rapid growth of London prime brokers financing Asian equities this year, after names like SK Hynix went vertical. London prime brokers financing Asian equities... it's almost as if someone had a specific bank in mind.

The Irony: Barclays Was The One That Said No To Leopold

Here's the twist that makes the story worse, not better. Per Bloomberg, Barclays had previously declined to take on Situational Awareness as a client because of concerns over concentration risk in the AI sector. Good call, as it turned out.

For those who missed it (i.e., regulators), Leopold Aschenbrenner's fund was running roughly 4x leverage via total return swaps, largely through Goldman, on a long AI infrastructure / short software book. When AI rolled over in July, the margin calls hit, and the fund dumped its entire public book on Ken Griffin's doorstep at roughly a 10% discount, collapsing from $45 billion to about $10 billion in a matter of days ("Situational Bewareness", Jul 30). Citadel, naturally, soared 6% in July on the firesale (Aug 5), and promptly flipped almost all of it (Aug 21). Our take at the time:

Archegos 2.0 it was.

*SITUATIONAL AWARENESS ASSETS SAID TO FALL TO $10 BILLION

Down from $45BN less than a month ago. Historic implosion.

Who is Archegos 3.0... there is still about $500BN in TRS excess leverage

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) July 30, 2026

So the "prudent" bank avoided the single most obvious blowup of the year, and still maxed out its Asian hedge fund lending to the point where it had to borrow capital from another desk to keep going. Which tells you that Leopold wasn't the problem; he was merely the most visible symptom of a market where everyone was levered to the same AI theme through the same few dealers' balance sheets.

Everyone Ran Out Of Balance Sheet

None of this should come as a surprise. Back in June, we highlighted Bloomberg strategist Simon White's warning that futures funding rates were exploding amid soaring total return swap demand (Jun 15). As White put it at the time:

"We are also seeing dealers offering a record amount of leveraged exposure to stocks via futures and total return swaps. Equity inventory on their balance sheet has risen to a high of $223 billion... This is demand driven, but also dealers' balance sheets are likely running into supply issues due to regulatory constraints." (emphasis ours)

Barclays has now confirmed the "supply issues" part, and how it got around them.

And we know how that story ended:

The chip/memory trade peaked THE DAY total return swap funding costs hit a record (as noted back in June).

The entire trade was all just leverage - largely from Situational Awareness - masking as narrative

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) August 23, 2026

Barclays isn't the only one bumping its head on the ceiling. Bloomberg notes that Goldman said earlier this month that demand for equities financing continues to exceed available industry capacity, with CFO Denis Coleman saying it allowed the bank to "remain selective in deploying resources." Back in July, Coleman said that in prime and FICC financing there was "far more demand across the segment than we're willing to engage." UBS CFO Todd Tuckner, meanwhile, said in July the bank's equities balance sheet was being used "more sparingly" for prime brokerage.

Put differently: Goldman and UBS publicly say they are rationing, and Barclays (which has spent years clawing its way up the prime brokerage league tables) is the one finding creative ways to fill the excess demand its rivals are turning away. When the biggest prime brokers on the Street are telling you demand exceeds what they're willing to finance, being the marginal lender who says yes is not usually a winning position.

How The Banks "Fixed" It: Make The Clients Short More

The most interesting detail in the Bloomberg piece is buried near the end: traders at Barclays, as at other banks including Goldman, worked with hedge fund clients to limit their balance sheet use by encouraging them to take more short positions, which lessen the burden on prime brokers' books (short proceeds help fund the longs internally).

And that is precisely what shows up in Goldman's own prime brokerage data. In his weekend note ("US EQUITIES - heightened demand for protection", Oct 18, available to pro subs), Goldman's Lee Coppersmith wrote:

"Our PB data showed US L/S net leverage fell 3.2pts last week, the largest weekly decline since Liberation Day and fourth-largest over the past five years. At 43.7%, net leverage now sits at a five-year low."

But here's the kicker:

"What's notable about the reduction in hedge fund net exposure is that essentially all of it since the end of July has come from an increase in shorts (not a reduction in longs) – h/t GS' Vincent Lin for the stats. Short exposure is now near five-year highs, while long exposure remains in the 53rd/72nd percentiles over the past three/five years… Said another way, managers have aggressively reduced their directional exposure, but haven't meaningfully reduced their long books." (emphasis ours)

The numbers: since July 31, long leverage is down a whopping 0.5pt to 128.8%, while short leverage is up 8.0pt to 85.1%, the 100th percentile over five years. Do the napkin math and gross leverage is roughly 214%, i.e., up, not down, since the Situational Awareness blowup.

Coppersmith is under no illusions about what that means if the pain continues:

"If the performance pressure continues, there's certainly scope for further de-grossing through long sales and short covering, but it's also worth recognizing just how much more defensive a lot of portfolios now look." (emphasis ours)

And the de-grossing has already started in the very names the prime brokers were financing in Asia:

"Global Tech saw its largest percentage net selling on record since 2016, with semis accounting for 57% of US technology net selling. A pretty remarkable unwind taking place across some of the most popular areas of the market." (emphasis ours)

UBS' trading desk sees the same setup. Here is desk trader Torsten Sippel in his weekly note (Oct 18, available to pro subs):

"This week's action looks like a positioning reset rather than broad equity liquidation, action very similar to the Situational Awareness driven unwind a couple months ago... That distinction matters given Hedge Fund net exposure has already fallen to the 30th percentile while gross remains above the 90th percentile on a five-year basis, leaving portfolios vulnerable to additional de-grossing if P&L pressure persists." (emphasis ours)

Translation: nobody actually de-risked. The longs are still there. The banks simply asked clients to bolt on more shorts so the net looks tamer and the prime broker's balance sheet usage looks lighter. That works beautifully... until longs and shorts move against the fund at the same time, which, as Leopold could tell you, is exactly what happened in July when AI infrastructure dumped and software ripped. A hedged book with 214% gross is still a 214% gross book.

The Payoff Comes Thursday

Why stretch so hard? Because it pays. Barclays' equities arm is expected to report £865 million ($1.2 billion) in Q3 revenue on Thursday, per Bloomberg consensus, which would be its best third quarter since at least 2009, the year after it bought Lehman's North American business. We are sure the Lehman reference is purely coincidental.

Prime brokerage has been the key driver of equities revenue across the Street this year, and the volatility that "fueled much of the surge in trading revenue" was itself largely a function of the leverage the prime brokers were extending. It's a closed loop: banks lend to funds, funds bid up AI, AI volatility generates trading revenue, revenue justifies more balance sheet for prime. Right up until the loop runs in reverse.

Bottom Line

Barclays' spokesperson insists the bank maintains "a disciplined approach to risk and returns." Perhaps. But discipline usually means that when you hit a limit, you stop, not that you hold an auction to borrow capital from the rates desk so you can keep financing the hottest trade in Asia. And when the "solution" to clients' bloated balance sheet usage is to have them pile on shorts, pushing short leverage to five-year highs while long books barely budge, the system isn't less levered; it's just levered in a way that looks better on the prime broker's capital report.

With the BoE already examining London prime brokers' Asian equity books, with UBS saying last week's de-grossing looked like a replay of the Situational Awareness unwind, and with gross leverage still near record, we suspect the question isn't whether Archegos 3.0 is out there, but which prime broker's balance sheet it's sitting on. The one that turned away Leopold may not be the one that turned away everyone.

We'll check back after Barclays reports on Thursday, and listen carefully for whether anyone on the call asks about Asia.

title: US Has Revoked More Than 300,000 Visas In Trump's Second Term
desc:
US Has Revoked More Than 300,000 Visas In Trump's Second Term

Authored by Troy Myers via The Epoch Times,

More than 300,000 foreign nationals have had their U.S. visas revoked since President Donald Trump entered office for a second term, due to criminal activity, fraud, or threats to national security.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said Oct. 20 that the pace of visa revocations by the Trump administration - as it reaches the two year mark of its four year term - has set a record.

"The Trump administration has revoked more visas at a faster pace than any administration in history," Pigott wrote in a post on X. "Let the message be clear: we have zero tolerance for foreigners here on visas who break the law, commit fraud, or undermine our national security."

A State Department official confirmed to The Epoch Times via email that the "vast majority" of revocations were due to criminal activity, public safety concerns, immigration violations, fraud, or other information indicating the foreign national was no longer eligible for a U.S. visa.

In 2025, the Bureau of Consular Affairs established a visa-vetting center in Washington, the official said, which led to the overturn of 23,000 of the 300,000 visas.

The majority of these were for criminal activity and other threats to public safety, the State Department official said, including 25 percent for assault and related offenses, 22 percent for driving under the influence, 7 percent for theft, and 7 percent for substance abuse or distribution. Other reasons for revocation included visa overstays and violations of student visa conditions.

Another 4,000 visa revocations targeted aliens who allegedly participated in facilitating birth tourism. These individuals attempted, at scale, to exploit U.S. law which grants citizenship to children born on U.S. soil.

The Supreme Court in a June 30 decision rejected the president's executive order that aimed to limit birthright citizenship from children of illegal foreign nationals and temporary visa holders.

Following that ruling, the Department of Justice (DOJ) directed its federal prosecutors to prioritize investigations into birth tourism schemes. Attorney General Todd Blanche told The Epoch Times earlier this month that the DOJ is coordinating with other federal agencies to tighten the visa screening process to combat birth tourism.

In August, after the Supreme Court's ruling, Trump issued two more limited orders for "Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship" and "Ending Birth Tourism" in an effort to restrict birthright citizenship consistent with historical exceptions recognized by the Supreme Court. The first of these has since been blocked in federal court.

The State Department did launch a birth tourism prevention task force in August, which has led to the revocation of visas in relation to birth tourism.

"One couple used a conference and a vacation trip to go shopping as cover stories to give birth to two children in the United States, lying about their travel purpose in two separate visa applications," the agency previously said.

A Record Pace

In January, the State Department announced it had revoked 100,000 visas in the first year of Trump's second term. By Aug. 10, the department said it had revoked another 75,000 visas in seven months.

Two months later on Oct. 1, that number increased by another 75,000 to a total of 250,000 visa revocations since January 2025.

"Every visa decision is a national security decision. Through continuous vetting on a scale never seen before, we are identifying and removing those who commit crimes, support terrorism, defraud Americans, or abuse our immigration system," Pigott previously told The Epoch Times. "A U.S. visa is a privilege, not a right - and if you violate the terms of that privilege, you will lose it."

Pigott's Oct. 20 announcement that revocations have exceeded 300,000 shows the State Department has further accelerated the pace in recent weeks, with the overall rate more than double the 2025 level.

"We are taking, and will continue to take, action to keep our borders, and our nation, secure," Pigott said on X.

The increasing amount of visa revocations is a sharp contrast from the previous administration. Pigott reported in January that the State Department, in the last year of the Biden administration, revoked approximately 40,000 visas.

A recent report by the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General found the Biden administration took little action on visa overstays due to limited resources and a policy implemented by then-Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas, which reshaped how immigration authorities targeted foreign nationals for enforcement action.

As a result, the report found that from fiscal years 2021 to 2024, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) received more than 3 million leads about possible alien overstays, with 104,049 classified as potential threats to national security and the American public.

Only 496 investigations were opened and eight foreign nationals arrested, the report showed.

title: Bloomberg Drops $80 Million On Democrats' Midterm Push: $24 Million To Everytown, $16 Million To House Majority PAC
desc:
Bloomberg Drops $80 Million On Democrats' Midterm Push: $24 Million To Everytown, $16 Million To House Majority PAC

Michael Bloomberg has sent about $80 million to Democratic causes in September and October, with at least $50 million aimed at House races and roughly $10 million more on the way, according to figures his team gave The New York Times. The filings that would confirm the gifts are not yet public: they are due this week, and some of the giving was still under way when the Times reported it Tuesday.

The biggest House checks went to two groups: $24 million to Everytown for Gun Safety, which he co-founded, and $16 million to House Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries. Bloomberg is now the largest disclosed donor to both groups. His Everytown money also freed up House Majority PAC funds for a roughly $10 million joint ad campaign for eight women House Democrats who have worked on gun safety.

The rest, as itemized: $5 million to the super PAC allied with the League of Conservation Voters, $3.5 million to a group electing Democratic scientists and doctors, $2.5 million to a super PAC backing Texas Senate nominee James Talarico, $8 million across about six battleground governor's races, and $2.5 million to a super PAC backing New York Gov. Kathy Hochul. Those seven gifts add up to $61.5 million, so about $18.5 million of the $80 million is not broken out by recipient, and one donation backing Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a possible 2028 candidate, carries no amount.

Howard Wolfson, Bloomberg's political adviser, said the donor "believes in participation in our democracy," that "resources matter in campaigns," and that he "expects a result." "The difference between 221 and 230, in terms of the House majority, really matters," Wolfson said. Jeffries said Bloomberg "played an incredibly instrumental role" in the 2018 midterms and that his support "will once again help Democrats flip the House."

Bloomberg, 84, is concentrating on the House because Democrats are favored to win it, while the Senate is seen as a toss-up and other big donors are shifting money there. Wolfson described him as a centrist who is worried about the party's leftward drift, particularly on Israel, and said he is not funding candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. He has not picked a 2028 candidate but would likely back one with a similar outlook.

The money lands against a Republican spending wave. Trump told reporters he plans to steer $400 million to $500 million to Republicans in the midterms, Reuters reported in September. The Trump-affiliated No Going Back PAC had reserved more than $74 million of ad time across 15 House races and Senate races in six states, MAGA Inc. put $10 million into the Texas Senate race, and Musk's America PAC has spent more than $7 million on digital ads, texts, calls and mailers. The Times describes Democrats as watching nervously while Musk and Trump's super PAC spend hundreds of millions, a question we took up earlier this month in asking whether Musk can rescue Republicans.

The party committees are lopsided. The Republican National Committee started September with about $126 million and was down to $76 million by Oct. 14, after sending more than $44 million to the National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, according to a Times report. The Democratic National Committee, by contrast, has reported negative cash on hand, counting debt, for nearly the entire 2025-26 cycle.

Bloomberg's fall budget resembles his 2018 midterm spending, which his team regards as his most effective campaign. That year he pledged at least $80 million in June and CBS News reported his total reached $110 million by late October, when Democrats took the House. Since then he has spent more than $1 billion on a failed 2020 presidential run and, this spring, $11 million to help Assembly member Micah Lasher win the Democratic primary for Jerrold Nadler's seat.

title: META Erases Most Afterhours Gains After CFO Warns "Significant Investment" Will Raise Serving Costs
desc:
META Erases Most Afterhours Gains After CFO Warns "Significant Investment" Will Raise Serving Costs

Update: We concluded our prompt earnings wrap (below), by saying that the question now is whether Zuck will scare investors on the call by noting that capex may raise much more." Well, CFO Susan Li did not help the case saying that “Muse's compute intensity means that expanding its user base will require significant investment, and we expect total serving costs to rise. At the same time, we expect to improve compute cost efficiency by more than 10-fold over the next year."

Translation: much more capex spending is coming, as in MUCH more, and not just the record $59BN implied by the 2026 capex guide...

... but much more in 2027 and beyond (sadly the company no longer provides guidance beyond this year). Which is a problem for a company which just joined Amazon in watching its free cash flow turn negative.

The stock did not like it, and after hitting a session high of $748.8, it has erased almost all after hours gains.

* * *

Earlier

In our preview of Meta's earnings, we laid out expectations...

  • Revenue estimate $63.32 billion (Bloomberg Consensus)
    • Advertising rev. estimate $61.82 billion
    • Family of Apps revenue estimate $62.75 billion
    • Reality Labs revenue estimate $517.7 million
    • Other revenue estimate $1.1 billion
  • Operating income estimate $20.28 billion
    • Family of Apps operating income estimate $23.96 billion
    • Reality Labs operating loss estimate $5.21 billion
  • Operating margin estimate 32.5%
  • EPS estimate $3.56
  • Ad impressions estimate +12.3%
    • Average price per ad estimate +11.2%
  • Average Family service users per day estimate 3.66 billion

... and also sketched a setup of what to expect from earnings:

  • expectations at 9/10,
  • positioning at 8/10,
  • Mag 7 exposure at a record,
  • an implied move that Goldman calls cheap,
  • a buyside bar for 2027 spending that's $50 billion above the Street,
  • a product whose growth may already have peaked, and...
  • an equity raise that the majority of the buyside expects as soon as the stock lets it.

Bloomberg points out that at 19x forward earnings, Meta is the second-cheapest Mag 7 stock after Nvidia. Well, it probably should be.

The bull case is that Zuckerberg beats, guides Q4 to $75 billion, drops a Muse DAU number (although with Claude just launching its own agents, it is about to get crowded) and keeps 2027 vague, and the stock grinds to $800 and the equity offering. The bear case is that he does all that and then says the words "notably larger" about 2027 capex. Judging by Meta's last two Q3 prints (-4% and -11% last October), and the last two prints overall (-9% and -8%), we know which one the tape has favored lately: the market keeps paying Meta for products and charging it for the bill.

With that in mind, here's what Meta reported moments ago for its Q3 quarter:

  • Revenue $64.60 billion, +26% y/y, beating estimate $63.33 billion
    • Advertising rev. $63.06 billion, +26% y/y, beating estimate $61.85 billion
    • Family of Apps revenue $64.16 billion, +26% y/y, beating estimate $62.75 billion
    • Reality Labs revenue $443 million, -5.7% y/y, missing estimate $517.7 million
    • Other revenue $1.10 billion, +59% y/y, in line with estimate $1.1 billion

  • Operating margin 20% vs. 40% y/y

  • Operating income $12.99 billion, -37% y/y, badly missing estimate $20.85 billion
    • Family of Apps operating income $17.12 billion, -31% y/y, beating estimate $23.3 billion
    • Reality Labs operating loss $4.13 billion vs. loss $4.43 billion y/y, estimate loss $5.13 billion
  • EPS $3.83 vs. $1.05 y/y, beating estimate $3.57
  • Operating margin 20% vs. 40% y/y

Here is how the numbers came relative to expectations:

There was some notable weakness in the company's core ad business: while average ad prices rose, impression growth actually collapsed.

  • Ad impressions +10% vs. +14% y/y, estimate +12.3%
  • Average price per ad +14% vs. +10% y/y, estimate +11.2%

A few more highlights from the quarter:

  • Meta Establishes New Non-Voting Class C Common Stock
  • Meta Lifts Expense Outlook to Incorporate $9.9B Legal Charge

Looking ahead, Meta shared the following Q4 revenue guidance: $73-76BN, vs sellside estimates of $73.6BN; recall in our preview we noted that the Street is at ~$73.5 billion (+24% FXN), with JPM's Schilsky saying investors "will tolerate no more than a 1-point FXN decel on the top end of the guidance range," so the expected guide is $72-75 billion. Deutsche hears a slightly lower top end, "roughly $74-74.5bn."

So Q4 guidance roughly in line with expectations... however that takes place at the expense of another capex increase, with Meta now expecting capex in the range of $135-$145, up from $130-$145 billion.

Doing some quick math here, we find that as a result of underspending on capex in 2026, META now has to spend as much as $59BN in one quarter, an absolute record considering its previous record was $34.9bn... this quarter. It will be interesting to see what META spends all this money on.

But wait, there's more because remember capex is just half the story since Meta can book data center spending either as capex (building it) or opex (leasing it from the likes of Crusoe), JPM said to watch the sum: "Buyside Consensus for 2027 Opex + Capex is in the range of $435B to $475B – that's a midpoint of $455B."

In this context, Meta raised its expense outlook to incorporate the $9.9 billion charge related to legal proceedings recognized in the third quarter, and now expects full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $175-179 billion. We will circle back once we calculate what all this means for the company's blended all in opex and capex for 2027 but it will be big.

title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid To End Hormone Treatments For Transgender Federal Inmates
desc:
Supreme Court Rejects Trump Bid To End Hormone Treatments For Transgender Federal Inmates

Authored by Matthew Vadum via The Epoch Times,

The Supreme Court on Oct. 21 declined to allow the Trump administration to immediately enforce a policy that would have curtailed transgender treatments in federal prisons.

The decision took the form of an unsigned order in Trump v. Kingdom. The court did not explain its ruling. Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito dissented from the order but did not explain why.

The Trump administration on Sept. 28 asked the Supreme Court to pause a nationwide injunction forcing the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) to keep providing hormone treatments and related services to inmates diagnosed with gender dysphoria.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer filed the emergency application that asked the justices to put on hold a federal district judge's order that blocks a BOP policy that shuts down transgender surgeries, hormone treatments, and social accommodations such as makeup and wigs.

The federal government says the policy, which is known as Program Statement 5260.01, is necessary for prison security.

The lead plaintiff in the underlying class action is Alishea Sophia Kingdom, a man who identifies as female.

Washington-based U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked the policy in June. He issued a written opinion saying that the program statement "amounts to arbitrary and capricious agency action" and that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on the merits of their claim under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The act is the federal law that establishes the rules for how agencies make and change policies. When an agency reverses course, a court can block the action if it believes the explanation falls short of the statute's requirements.

Lamberth directed the BOP to keep providing hormone treatments and related accommodations to inmates who have a gender dysphoria diagnosis and to inmates who later receive one. A panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit later declined to stay Lamberth's order.

Sauer said Lamberth's ruling "denied prison administrators the substantial deference they are due." If the preliminary injunction remains, it interferes with administrators' expert judgment about how to administer federal prisons, he said.

For almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021.

He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. title: "F**k You And Your Sh**ty Values": Adam Corolla Unloads On SF Mayor
desc:
"F**k You And Your Sh**ty Values": Adam Corolla Unloads On SF Mayor

Adam Carolla went after San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie in response to a CNN interview last week - telling the mayor: "F**K YOU AND YOUR F**KING SH*TTY VALUES!"

Lurie told CNN's Dana Bash that San Francisco "lost its way" and was "entrapped in our progressive values," according to the Fox News report carried by WFMD. He pointed to 810 overdose deaths in San Francisco three years ago and about 30,000 car break-ins, which he said have since dropped 90%. The moderate Democrat, an heir to the Levi Strauss fortune who beat incumbent London Breed in 2024, said he still backs progressive causes such as caring for immigrants and the LGBTQ+ community, but not tolerating drug use on the street or theft from small businesses: "There's nothing progressive about that."

Adam Carolla DETONATES after San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie admits the city "lost its way" on progressive values.

"F**K YOU AND YOUR F**KING SH*TTY VALUES."

He said what millions are thinking. The f-bombs are completely appropriate here.

CAROLLA: "Your ideas SUCK. Your... pic.twitter.com/hXFkX40xBm

— The Vigilant Fox 🦊 (@VigilantFox) October 16, 2026

In the clip, Carolla says: "Your ideas SUCK. Your progressive ideas SUCK. They ruin cities." He adds: "A whole bunch of people OD'd because of your sh*tty f**king values."

Modernity's write-up relays his boat analogy: one progressive captain lets the water in, the next pumps half of it out, and the city is told to be grateful because the boat is sinking more slowly. He names other cities he says went the same way: "San Diego's turned to sh*t. Austin's turned to sh*t. LA's turned to sh*t."

His alternative is a mayor who treats the job as an administrator's. "You're running a f**king city. You have a budget. That's it. Crime, statistics, school, education, traffic. I don't give a f**k about your values," he says, and ends with: "MY VALUES ARE GET THE F**K UP AND GO TO WORK AND SHUT UP."

Lurie's remarks drew support across party lines. Fox News Digital quoted Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff saying "Lurie is right," and the Fox report noted that President Trump said at a March cabinet meeting, "I know they have a mayor who's trying very hard."

title: 45% Of College Students Justify Violence To Stop 'Hate Speech': Survey
desc:
45% Of College Students Justify Violence To Stop 'Hate Speech': Survey

Authored by Bryan Hyde via American Greatness,

A new survey finds that nearly half of undergraduate students support censorship, shout-downs, and physical violence to suppress what they consider “hate speech” or offensive ideas.

Fox News reports that the 2026 National Undergraduate Student Survey, released this month by the Buckley Institute, shows that 45 percent of undergraduate students surveyed believe physical violence can be justified to stop so-called hate speech. That number is up 6 points from 2025 and ties the all-time record set in 2023.

The survey, which polled 803 full-time undergraduate students at four-year public and private colleges across the United States, revealed several record-high metrics concerning free expression on campus, according to Yahoo.

A little over a year after Charlie Kirk’s assassination, 1 in 4 college students think “It should not be a surprise that his words had consequences.”

Our new survey found increasing undergrad comfort with violence and criminal prosecution for speech they don’t like. https://t.co/mxeoZ4up8Z

— Buckley Institute (@BuckleyInst) October 18, 2026

Other takeaways from the survey were that 46 percent of students support shout downs and 40 percent believe that offensive speech should be subject to criminal prosecution.

Some 42 percent of respondents said that political comments they disagree with can be harmful to their mental health, up 4 points from last year; the highest reading in the 5 years this question has been monitored.

The findings prompted Cornerstone University President Dr. Gerson Moreno-Riaño to warn that higher education has “lost its way.”

Moreno-Riaño told Fox News Digital:

American colleges and universities for a long time now have really ceased to form students morally and are teaching resentment, teaching grievance politics, teaching violent entitlement. So, when graduates leave these universities, they leave with that. They’re not leaving with a moral formation of their hearts, their minds, their lives. They’re leaving with resentment.

Moreno-Riaño also cautioned that many colleges and universities are preparing “socialists and Marxists” who want entitlement and to “destroy the system” rather than “build it, make it, refine it and improve it.”

The Cornerstone University president also stressed that American higher education “has to shift,” saying it needs to “take moral formation seriously and not be grounded in entitlement and grievance culture.”

The Buckley Institute survey was conducted online between Sept. 5 and Sept. 14 by Inquire LLC and included 803 full-time undergraduate students under age 25 attending four-year public or private colleges and universities.

title: META Jumps After Q3 Earnings Beat, Boosts Guidance
desc:
META Jumps After Q3 Earnings Beat, Boosts Guidance

In our preview of Meta's earnings, we laid out expectations...

  • Revenue estimate $63.32 billion (Bloomberg Consensus)
    • Advertising rev. estimate $61.82 billion
    • Family of Apps revenue estimate $62.75 billion
    • Reality Labs revenue estimate $517.7 million
    • Other revenue estimate $1.1 billion
  • Operating income estimate $20.28 billion
    • Family of Apps operating income estimate $23.96 billion
    • Reality Labs operating loss estimate $5.21 billion
  • Operating margin estimate 32.5%
  • EPS estimate $3.56
  • Ad impressions estimate +12.3%
    • Average price per ad estimate +11.2%
  • Average Family service users per day estimate 3.66 billion

... and also sketched a setup of what to expect from earnings:

  • expectations at 9/10,
  • positioning at 8/10,
  • Mag 7 exposure at a record,
  • an implied move that Goldman calls cheap,
  • a buyside bar for 2027 spending that's $50 billion above the Street,
  • a product whose growth may already have peaked, and...
  • an equity raise that the majority of the buyside expects as soon as the stock lets it.

Bloomberg points out that at 19x forward earnings, Meta is the second-cheapest Mag 7 stock after Nvidia. Well, it probably should be.

The bull case is that Zuckerberg beats, guides Q4 to $75 billion, drops a Muse DAU number (although with Claude just launching its own agents, it is about to get crowded) and keeps 2027 vague, and the stock grinds to $800 and the equity offering. The bear case is that he does all that and then says the words "notably larger" about 2027 capex. Judging by Meta's last two Q3 prints (-4% and -11% last October), and the last two prints overall (-9% and -8%), we know which one the tape has favored lately: the market keeps paying Meta for products and charging it for the bill.

With that in mind, here's what Meta reported moments ago for its Q3 quarter:

  • Revenue $64.60 billion, +26% y/y, beating estimate $63.33 billion
    • Advertising rev. $63.06 billion, +26% y/y, beating estimate $61.85 billion
    • Family of Apps revenue $64.16 billion, +26% y/y, beating estimate $62.75 billion
    • Reality Labs revenue $443 million, -5.7% y/y, missing estimate $517.7 million
    • Other revenue $1.10 billion, +59% y/y, in line with estimate $1.1 billion

  • Operating margin 20% vs. 40% y/y

  • Operating income $12.99 billion, -37% y/y, badly missing estimate $20.85 billion
    • Family of Apps operating income $17.12 billion, -31% y/y, beating estimate $23.3 billion
    • Reality Labs operating loss $4.13 billion vs. loss $4.43 billion y/y, estimate loss $5.13 billion
  • EPS $3.83 vs. $1.05 y/y, beating estimate $3.57
  • Ad impressions +10% vs. +14% y/y, estimate +12.3%
    • Average price per ad +14% vs. +10% y/y, estimate +11.2%
  • Average Family service users per day 3.64 billion, +2.8% y/y, estimate 3.66 billion
  • Operating margin 20% vs. 40% y/y

A few more highlights from the quarter:

  • Meta Establishes New Non-Voting Class C Common Stock
  • Meta Lifts Expense Outlook to Incorporate $9.9B Legal Charge

Looking ahead, Meta shared the following Q4 revenue guidance: $73-76BN, vs sellside estimates of $73.6BN; recall in our preview we noted that the Street is at ~$73.5 billion (+24% FXN), with JPM's Schilsky saying investors "will tolerate no more than a 1-point FXN decel on the top end of the guidance range," so the expected guide is $72-75 billion. Deutsche hears a slightly lower top end, "roughly $74-74.5bn."

So Q4 guidance roughly in line with expectations... however that takes place at the expense of another capex increase, with Meta now expecting capex in the range of $135-$145, up from $130-$145 billion.

Some more from the company:

  • Meta Establishes New Non-Voting Class C Common Stock
  • Meta Lifts Expense Outlook to Incorporate $9.9B Legal Charge
  • "Excluding the third quarter legal charge, we continue to expect 2026 operating income to be above 2025 operating income."
  • "We now expect full year 2026 total expenses to be in the range of $175-179 billion."
  • "We expect fourth quarter 2026 total revenue to be in the range of $73-76 billion."

To the last point, news broke today that Meta plans to introduce a new class of non-voting stock that it could use to fund its heavy spending on artificial intelligence, according to a Semafor report. The plan could be announced as soon as Wednesday during the company’s quarterly earnings report, the publication said, enabling Meta to use the stock to fund acquisitions and AI spending without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s control of the company.

Following the earnings release, the initial stock reaction was muted but shares have now picked a direction - the stock was up 4% after hours, before easing back on the gains, and up about 2% at last check.

The question now is whether Zuck will scare investors on the call by noting that capex may raise much more...

title: Tesla Gains On EPS Beat, Crushes FCF Estimates... By Spending $3 Billion Less Than Expected
desc:
Tesla Gains On EPS Beat, Crushes FCF Estimates... By Spending $3 Billion Less Than Expected

Ahead of today's print, the Street had braced for Tesla (TSLA) to burn about $5 billion in the quarter. Instead it generated $1.5 billion.

Tesla reported Q3 results after the close and, at least at first glance, it was a clean beat: adjusted EPS of 48 cents topped the 44 cent Bloomberg consensus, revenue of $28.05 billion came in bang in line (and flat from a year ago), and free cash flow of $1.53 billion crushed the consensus estimate of negative $4.99 billion. That's a swing of roughly $6.5 billion vs expectations, which we flagged the moment it hit the tape:

*TESLA 3Q FREE CASH FLOW $1.53B, EST. NEGATIVE $4.99B

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 21, 2026

But before anyone pops the champagne, there is a catch. Actually, several. Below we look at what drove the "beat", where the money is going, and why the market couldn't care less about any of it with a SpaceX merger hanging overhead.

The CapEx That Wasn't

Let's start with the headline number. Tesla's CapEx came in at $4.73 billion in Q3, more than double the $2.25 billion from a year ago, but well below the $5.79 billion spent in Q2 and, more importantly, $3 billion short of the $7.77 billion consensus compiled by Tesla itself (which had also penciled in FCF of negative $4.51 billion).

In other words, roughly half of the FCF "beat" was simply money that Tesla didn't spend this quarter. Don't get us wrong: generating cash is better than burning it. But a cash beat that comes from deferred spending tends to come back to bite, usually in the very next quarter.

And bite it probably will. Recall that back in April Musk said Tesla would spend $25 billion on CapEx in 2026, a number which, as we pointed out after Q2 earnings, the company was nowhere near tracking. With $8.28 billion spent in H1 and another $4.73 billion in Q3, Tesla has spent about $13 billion through September. Napkin math says hitting the $25 billion target requires roughly $12 billion in Q4 alone (or about 2.5x what it spent this quarter). Either the guide gets cut on tonight's call, or Q4 free cash flow gets ugly. Pick one.

Paying For The Robot Future

Below the gross profit line, the story looked very much like Q2: Tesla is pouring money into what it now calls "Super Intelligence", Optimus and the Cybercab, and the spending is growing far faster than the profits that are supposed to fund it.

  • Operating expenses jumped 39% YoY to $4.78 billion, with R&D alone up 69% to $2.76 billion.

  • Stock-based comp, which now includes Elon's 2025 pay package, hit $1.17 billion, up from $663 million a year ago.

  • As a result, operating income fell 56% to $718 million, for an operating margin of just 2.6%, vs 5.8% a year ago.

Granted, that's an improvement from the dismal 1.4% margin in Q2, which sent the stock down about 15% the next day. But a 2.6% operating margin for a company with a $1.5 trillion market cap is... well, let's just say it's not why anyone owns the stock.

GAAP net income fell 43% to $787 million, or 22 cents a share, and even that got some help from a $288 million unrealized gain on Tesla's bitcoin, partly offset by a $142 million unrealized loss on its SpaceX stake. Diversification at its finest.

Margins Bounce... But "Batteries, Not Buyers"

The genuinely good news was on gross margin. Total gross margin rose to 19.6% from 18.0% a year ago (and 16.8% in Q2), while the number everyone watches - automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits - rebounded to 18.1% from 16.3% in Q2 and 15.4% a year ago. Tesla credited better regional and product mix and more FSD subscription revenue, partly offset by (once again) lower average selling prices.

That last point is worth dwelling on, because Tesla has a new explanation for its flat sales. According to the shareholder deck, battery availability "continued to be the limiting factor" on auto volumes, and the company says it exited Q3 with its biggest passenger-vehicle backlog in four years.

Supply constrained? Perhaps. But deliveries were still down 2% YoY, Tesla delivered 22,141 more cars than it built (draining inventory to 11 days of supply from 15), "other models" (Cybertruck, Semi, S and X) collapsed 48%, and ASPs fell again. Translation: supply-constrained automakers don't usually cut prices.

Elsewhere:

  • Regulatory credits - once Tesla's favorite cash cow - shrank 73% YoY to just $113 million, and with automakers no longer paying federal fuel-economy penalties, that line isn't coming back.

  • Energy was the weak spot: revenue fell 16% to $2.88 billion (Tesla blamed tariff-related customer refunds) even as deployments rose 10% to 13.7 GWh, still short of the ~15.9 GWh analysts expected. Segment gross margin jumped to 33% from 20% in Q2.

  • Services and other was the bright spot, with revenue up 33% to $4.61 billion and record gross profit of $734 million.

  • Autonomy: active FSD subscriptions hit 1.74 million, up 67% (although that count includes upfront purchases, as defined in Musk's 2025 pay package... funny how that works), while Robotaxi crossed roughly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles, a month after the Cybercab joined the Austin fleet.

Tesla ended the quarter with $45.4 billion in cash and investments, which should come in handy if that $25 billion CapEx plan is still a thing.

Nobody Is Trading The Earnings Anyway

Which brings us to the real story. For all the line-item drama above, the stock didn't rip: after closing up 3.4% at $386.47, TSLA was up about another 1% after hours at last check (admittedly breaking to 3 month highs)...

And it's not hard to see why.

Just one day earlier, SpaceX reported a blowout quarter and Musk confirmed that both companies have formed special committees to discuss a merger. As Goldman's consumer desk put it in its morning note (available to pro subs):

Elon Musk endorsed a potential SpaceX–Tesla combination, which would be the largest corporate merger ever, as both boards formed independent special committees; no terms are settled, and Musk cautioned Tesla shareholder support may be difficult.

The desk also noted that the $1.5 trillion carmaker remains down 17% YTD, while its would-be partner trades at a $2 trillion valuation. Meanwhile, Goldman's prime book reports that Mag 7 net exposure "has risen to a new record high", even as hedge funds dumped tech at a record pace over the past two weeks. In short: everyone is already in the trade.

For those keeping score, here is what Musk said about a merger just three months ago, on the Q2 call:

*MUSK SEES MORE OVERLAP BETWEEN TESLA, SPACEX

*MUSK SAYS CAN'T COMMENT ON POTENTIAL MERGER ON EARNINGS CALL

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) July 22, 2026

Something tells us tonight's call will be a little more talkative.

The Roadster Was The Easy Part

Let's be fair: by Tesla's recent standards, this was a decent quarter. Gross margins are recovering, the company is cash-flow positive, and the core auto business has stopped shrinking (for now). But strip out the capex shortfall, and Tesla is a business whose operating income has halved in a year to fund a robot future that, much like last week's flying Roadster, keeps arriving "soon".

The bulls will say none of that matters if Tesla becomes the earthbound arm of a $3.5 trillion Musk conglomerate. And they may be right, at least until the merger math has to be done in a proxy statement. But a company that needs to spend $12 billion in one quarter to hit its own capex target, while its legacy cash cow (regulatory credits) dies, is going to need SpaceX a lot more than SpaceX needs it.

Of course, what really matters with this stock is what Musk says during the call at 1730ET.
