title: "Pure Evil": Musk Goes Nuclear On Talarico As George W.'s Brother Does 180
desc:
"Pure Evil": Musk Goes Nuclear On Talarico As George W.'s Brother Does 180

In Texas, everything is bigger. That includes the money, the insults and the family feuds.

Two weeks before Election Day, with early voting already under way, the most expensive Senate race in US history got its two most viral moments on the same day. Shortly before 2pm ET, the world's richest man, who has bankrolled much of the GOP effort to save Ken Paxton, quote-tweeted a four-minute supercut of Democrat James Talarico and delivered his verdict: Pure Evil

Talarico would vote to take away your kids and transition them, not just in Texas, but nationwide.

Pure evil. https://t.co/3klyOjV4PC

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 21, 2026

Hours earlier, from the other end of the Republican family tree, came this:

Neil Bush is trending after announcing he voted early for Democrat James Talarico over Ken Paxton.

In a Facebook post, the son of George H.W. Bush knocked Paxton for challenging the 2020 election and for his impeachment, and praised Talarico for civility and humility.

Texans... pic.twitter.com/XOhZ7f6Zcx

— Gunther Eagleman™ (@GuntherEagleman) October 21, 2026

In other words, the GOP establishment and the GOP's biggest donor are now openly campaigning on opposite sides of the same Senate seat. Below we walk through what Neil Bush actually said, how much money Musk has put behind Paxton, and why the race that decides the Senate may come down to who can persuade a Texan the other guy is the real threat.

"Character Matters More Than Party"

Neil Bush, 71, son of the late President George H.W. Bush and chair of his father's Points of Light nonprofit, wrote on Facebook on Tuesday, as first reported by Newsweek:

"I voted early today, and I voted for James Talarico for the United States Senate... I have been deeply troubled by Paxton's conduct as Texas Attorney General, particularly his decision to challenge the results of the 2020 presidential election in other states in an effort to help Donald Trump remain in power."

He also brought up Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the GOP-controlled Texas House (Paxton was acquitted by the state Senate) and said, per The Hill, that Trump has done "enormous damage to the Republican party." He also gushed that Talarico's "faith appears to be a deeply rooted source of humility, compassion, and conviction rather than a political weapon."

It isn't just Neil. According to the Texas Gazette, FEC filings show George W.'s daughter Barbara gave $2,500 to Lone Star Rising PAC, the main pro-Talarico super PAC. The paper also cited a Fort Worth Star-Telegram column reporting that the former president took part in a Dallas fundraiser for six other GOP Senate candidates, with Paxton left off the list. Family dinners must be fun.

The $158 Million Rescue

Musk isn't just posting. As regular readers will recall from our Oct. 13 look at whether Elon can rescue Republicans in November, Musk put $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund in September, and the money went straight to Texas PAC, the group backing Paxton. Reuters added the latest numbers on Wednesday:

*OUTSIDE GROUPS BACKING PAXTON HAVE SPENT ABOUT $239M, MORE THAN FIVE TIMES THE ~$45M BY LARGEST DEM-ALIGNED GROUPS

*COMBINED AD SPENDING IN RACE TOPS $500M, ON PACE FOR MOST EXPENSIVE SENATE CONTEST EVER

Talarico has made up the gap the old-fashioned way. His campaign says it raised $64 million from July through September, more than triple Paxton's haul, with 97% of donations under $100. Republican donor Dan Eberhart summed up the GOP view to Reuters: "I think the cavalry arrived just in the nick of time for Paxton."

"If The Terms Are Right"

And the candidate the cavalry is riding in to save? When he was asked about debating Talarico this week, Paxton came up with an unusual condition:

Q: Do you want to debate James Talarico?

Ken Paxton: I- Look. I-if the terms are right

Q: What are your terms?

Paxton: I don't wanna end up with a CNN reporter on the debate. I don't- I don't know what all the terms are. pic.twitter.com/eGM7WaPYzv

— Headquarters (@HQNewsNow) October 21, 2026

Talarico's answer, per TMZ, was to offer to hold the debate on TMZ. Put differently, the Democrat will debate anywhere, while the Republican wants the moderator vetted first. That's not a great look when your own side's message is that the other guy is the one hiding something. (Readers will recall Paxton's camp made hay of Talarico's two-week flu disappearance earlier this month.)

To Be Fair...

Musk's supporters will say the supercut speaks for itself. Every quote in it is attributed to Talarico, and lines like "God is non-binary" and "Prison is violence" are hard to square with the "pragmatic moderate" image Neil Bush is selling. For an electorate that has backed Republicans statewide for three decades, the culture-war framing may be exactly the right closing argument, which is presumably why the Musk-backed PAC has been running on it for weeks.

The polls are a coin toss. A University of Houston Hobby School poll (Oct. 10-15) had Talarico up 48-46, and CBS/YouGov (Oct. 8-16) had him ahead 51-49. Both are inside the margin of error. Close polls in Texas have also been false dawns for Democrats before.

Bushes, Billionaires And Ballots

The Paxton camp's line is that the old guard always sides with the Democrat over the fighter, and Musk is simply calling out a radical. Our summary is less so: when a Bush endorses the Democrat, the richest man alive calls that Democrat "pure evil," and the Republican won't debate unless CNN is barred, the GOP is running two campaigns in Texas at once, and they don't agree with each other. Texas could decide the Senate majority. Early voting ends Oct. 30, Election Day is Nov. 3, and we'll find out whether $239 million of outside money beats a $2,500 check from a Bush granddaughter.

Then again, if Talarico wins, Elon will have spent $158 million to prove Neil Bush right.

title: "Polished But Rough": First Major Review Casts Doubt On Foldable iPhone Duo's Mass Adoption
desc:
"Polished But Rough": First Major Review Casts Doubt On Foldable iPhone Duo's Mass Adoption

Tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee, who has more than 21 million subscribers, offered a mixed first take on Apple's foldable iPhone Duo ahead of its Friday release, describing the device as "very polished around the edges, but kind of rough in the middle."

Brownlee's review of Apple's first foldable iPhone may present a hurdle to adoption. At more than $2,000, the Duo's first-generation shortcomings could make buyers reluctant to pay the hefty premium, prompting some to wait for a second generation.

"It's $2,000 to get an iPad mini that can fit in your pocket. 120 Hz iPad Mini OLED fits in your pocket. Have you ever wanted that? They made it. They did it. Great. This is the first generation. It's made for you. But also, yeah, it is it is polished but rough," Brownlee noted.

The Duo is slightly thicker and heavier than the latest Samsung Galaxy Z Fold, a difference Brownlee said "makes a big difference in daily use."

After testing the Duo for a week, he said, "you would be happy if it were 20% lighter."

Brownlee pointed out that the battery capacity is about 4,900 mAh, split across the two halves. With typical mixed use (roughly 75% closed and 25% open), Brownlee called it a "very efficient phone" and "an all-day phone and then some," regularly finishing the day with more than 30% battery remaining.

The dual rear cameras (48 MP main and ultra-wide) are "right on par with the rest of the foldables" and "solid" most of the time, though the smaller main sensor gets noisier in weaker light and there is no optical zoom, he explained.

He continued, "The app situation on the iPhone Duo is its biggest downside right now."

"I think after the learning curve and getting used to not having Face ID, this is a really fun phone to use," he added.

Brownlee's verdict is mixed:

If you are the iPhone filmmaker who wants the absolute best cameras to go shoot their next thing, no. Uh if you're the type of person who breaks your phone every like nine months cuz you drop it all the time, yep, probably no. But if the $2,000 or the difference between 35 and 55 bucks a month doesn't mean much to you and you just kind of like the idea and want to jump in, I think after the learning curve and and getting used to not having Face ID, this is a really fun phone to use.

And it's really just cuz that polish, that polish around the edges goes a long way towards the fun factor. So, the awesome animations, the incredible hinge, the wonderful inside display, like all of that is just really nice and it hides a little bit of the rough core. Like, it will feel a little heavy sometimes and not all your favorite apps will be updated right out the box, but it is fun.

Apple can't completely engineer their way around the compromises of this form factor, like the slightly worse battery and the slightly worse speakers and the slightly worse cameras. Like, that's just physics. But what they have done is an admirable job with their first generation. Now, I'm just going to have to cross my fingers that second generation actually listens to some of that core feedback cuz that could be an amazing phone.

Watch The Duo Review Here Before Buying

Last Friday, when preorders for the Duo opened, we pointed out the incredible initial demand as delivery estimates slipped further and further beyond this Friday by the minute.

As of Wednesday afternoon, the Duo's estimated delivery date is January 22.

The question remains whether the Duo, at a base price of $2,000, can achieve mass adoption, given that Tim Cook's $3,400 Vision Pro was a total disaster. Now it's John Ternus' turn to prove to investors that Apple still has demand for its premium products.

title: 1% Of Companies Account For 80% Of OpenAI And Anthropic Spending - And It Just Stalled
desc:
1% Of Companies Account For 80% Of OpenAI And Anthropic Spending - And It Just Stalled

Just 1% of companies account for 80% of all business spending on OpenAI and Anthropic, according to corporate card giant Ramp, which tracks payments across more than 70,000 U.S. businesses. Ramp lead economist Ara Kharazian, who flagged the figure in early September, noted that spending on the two AI labs is more concentrated than in any other software category the firm tracks.

Per capita, the biggest spenders are overwhelmingly venture-backed. According to Ramp's summer report, the median VC-backed startup spent $76 per employee per month on AI - more than ten times the $7 spent at private equity-backed firms.

That top-heavy dynamic mirrors what YipitData uncovered at Anthropic specifically: the lab's top 1% of customers generated 46% of its revenue in August, nearly doubling from 25% a year earlier. How many of those whale customers, we asked at the time, are funded by the very same VCs backing Anthropic?

Anthropic's IPO prospectus - the updated version of which we dissected yesterday - confirms the concentration at the very top: just two unnamed customers generated nearly a quarter of its 2025 revenue, according to Reuters. Their identities aren't hard to guess. Last year, two AI coding tools - Cursor and Microsoft's GitHub Copilot - drove roughly $1.2 billion of Anthropic's $5 billion annualized revenue run-rate, as VentureBeat reported.

Follow the money. Cursor's parent company, Anysphere, raised $2.3 billion at a $29.3 billion valuation last November in a round co-led by Accel and Coatue, alongside Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia, and Google. Three months later, Coatue and Singapore's GIC led Anthropic's massive $30 billion Series G, with Nvidia again participating. Coatue's cash flows into Cursor, Cursor spends it on Claude tokens, those tokens book as Anthropic revenue, and that revenue underwrites the markups on Coatue's Anthropic stake.

Even the scorekeeper is inside the loop. Ramp itself raised $1.85 billion at a $60 billion valuation last week in a round led by Dragoneer, Thrive, Founders Fund, Sands Capital, and Avenir Growth. Its cap table also features Coatue, D1, ICONIQ, GIC, Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, General Catalyst, and Lightspeed - every single one of which, alongside Dragoneer and Founders Fund, backed Anthropic's Series G.

Volumes Up, Dollars Flat

Yet it is Ramp's own economist who is documenting the cracks in the facade. In his October AI Index - pointedly titled "Cracks in the AI Thesis Part 3" - Kharazian reported that the top 1% of AI-spending firms shelled out $9,568 per employee in September. While that was up 11.7% from August, it remained 3.1% below July's peak of $9,873.

Across the broader cohort, the stall is even starker. In August and September, Ramp recorded "two straight months of virtually no growth in token spend," even as raw token volumes continued to climb.

Total dollar spend did eke out a new high in early October, but cleared its previous August peak by a paltry 1.5%.

Source: Ramp Rate

The culprit, according to Kharazian, is deflation: "the main driver is price declines at the frontier, in addition to efficiency and quality improvements for models across intelligence levels, that are driving the blended price per million tokens down."

Source: Ramp Rate

Nor have the AI labs been able to lock in their biggest customers. Asked whether OpenAI and Anthropic are using enterprise contracts to guarantee revenue, Kharazian noted that buyers hold all the leverage. Enterprise deals are rarely signed on the assumption of higher-than-normal spend, and when they are, "the labs are willing to provide concessions in the form of discounts on models from the sticker price." His takeaway: "These contracts could contribute to price cuts without driving additional volume."

The customer base isn't widening much, either. Paid AI adoption across Ramp's corporate network nudged up just 0.62 percentage points to 55.9% in September. "It feels like we're at the top of the S-curve," Kharazian wrote, "where the growth in the market will have to come from more intense adoption rather than more customers."

Source: Ramp Rate

Anthropic Joins The Price War

Meanwhile, Anthropic's realized token price has been cut in half in just a month. The Ornn Anthropic Token Price Index - which measures the actual dollars customers pay per token consumed - has cratered to $0.83 per million tokens from over $1.70 in mid-September, marking a record low since the benchmark launched in June.

Even after that plunge, Anthropic remains pricier than OpenAI, whose index sits at $0.45. OpenAI's realized pricing collapsed in late July after it slashed rates on its GPT-5.6 Luna and Terra models by up to 80% - just three days after Chinese lab Moonshot released the open weights for Kimi K3, the model blamed for sending chip stocks into a bear market earlier that month. OpenAI has since reportedly leaned toward delaying its IPO until 2027.

Jevons Isn't Riding To The Rescue

Jevon is an offset and total demand is rising... until it hits physical constraints of hundreds of delayed or canceled data centers. https://t.co/BqONarz80n

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 14, 2026

The bulls' reflex answer to relentless price cuts is Jevons paradox: make tokens cheap enough, and usage will explode so fast that total revenue rises anyway. The data isn't cooperating. In a Sept. 25 note, Goldman Sachs warned that "token demand growth will need to outpace declining token prices to support continued growth in investment spending," noting that while "frontier models are currently a key source of demand for hyperscaler compute," cheap open-source rivals are rapidly gaining ground. By Goldman's estimate - built on Anera and OpenRouter data - total token demand has surged roughly 18-fold since December, but demand for high-margin frontier models has grown only half as fast.

That margin squeeze is now flowing directly upstream to the companies building the data centers. Goldman calculates that realized return on invested capital (ROIC) across Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle has fallen from 40% to 25% - the lowest reading in its dataset going back to 2016.

On Tuesday - the same day Citadel's Ken Griffin told Bloomberg that markets are "almost certainly" in an AI bubble - Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok diagnosed the underlying demand problem. "Silicon Valley operates on the premise that compute demand is unlimited, yet the recent slowdown in token spending growth suggests that this appetite may exist only when compute is effectively free," Slok wrote, citing Ramp's figures. Instead of inelastic hunger, compute faces "a flat, highly price-sensitive demand curve, where even modest changes in token prices can drive buyers to throttle usage or substitute cheap open-source alternatives."

"Ultimately, the number-one variable governing the viability of data center construction models is not physical capacity or power; it is the actual price users are willing to pay for the compute being built," Slok concluded. Corporate buyers will only pay a premium if they can translate tokens into "higher top-line growth, bigger profit margins or substantial cost savings, little of which is showing up at scale yet. Maybe that will come in the future. Maybe not."

Back in June, Ramp product director Adam Sommer boasted to a New York panel that "our largest AI spenders at Ramp are seeing their spend double month-over-month for the last several months." Three months later, the top 1% were spending less per employee than they had in July.

title: Pollster Cited By NY Times, Other Outlets Admits It's Fake
desc:
Pollster Cited By NY Times, Other Outlets Admits It's Fake

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

A purported company whose polls were listed by a slew of outlets, including The New York Times, has said that all but one of its surveys were not real.

Wedgewood Polling said in a statement on Oct. 20 that it was developed by people who previously worked in the poll sector and wondered how easy it would be for a fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and "expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary."

The entity said that its surveys often did not have any real data behind them, but they were nonetheless included in poll averages by the NY Times and some other outlets.

"Our fabricated numbers were given instant credibility across national media platforms - including being cited on air and in reporting by outlets such as MS Now," Wedgewood Polling said. "The ease with which unverified figures were absorbed into mainstream political narratives highlights a systemic breakdown in media vetting and data aggregation."

The surveys largely favored Democrats, including having Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Republican candidate Mike Rogers in the race for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan.

Wedgewood Polling conducted a single legitimate poll, in Nebraska, that served as a baseline to compare against fake data.

Wedgewood Polling said it did not intend to mislead the public or sway an election, and that the purpose was to spark changes in the polling and media industries.

Decision Desk HQ said on X on Wednesday that it removed 17 polls from Wedgewood Polling in light of the company's admission.

"As polling and averages are a component of our forecast model, we have rerun the model and all of our forecasts now reflect the removal of the fraudulent data," Decision Desk said. "The removal of these polls has not changed the projected seat totals or chamber control probabilities in the Senate or House."

Zachary Donnini, head of data science at VoteHub, another poll aggregator, said on X on Tuesday that he contacted Wedgewood Polling's head pollster after the company first appeared, and that the individual said he was a college student who had experience in the polling space. The conversation led to VoteHub including polls from the company on its website.

"A few years ago, I was a college student following politics as a hobby myself, so I try to give people in that position the benefit of the doubt," Donnini said. "It's disappointing to see how this has unfolded, because it's going to be a ... lot harder for the next college kid who's actually well-intentioned and super into politics to break into the space after this."

FiftyPlusOne, which had also included Wedgewood Polling surveys, said on Tuesday that it had sent questions about the polls to the company prior to the admission that most of its polls were fake. It said the questions prompted the disclosure.

title: Are Bonds Pricing In A Fed Policy Mistake?
desc:
Are Bonds Pricing In A Fed Policy Mistake?

Authored by Michael Lebowitz via RealInvestmentAdvice.com,

Imagine someone looking into their crystal ball and telling you at the beginning of October that the coming September CPI data would be higher than expected, and producer prices (PPI) would rise 1.3% for the month, well above the 0.5% forecast. On top of the bad inflation news, they also said more inflation pressure was brewing, with crude oil prices rising $10 through the first two weeks of the month. Based on that foresight, where would you guess the 10-year Treasury yield would be? To help you answer, the ten-year US Treasury yield was flirting with 5.25% on October 1. We bet most professional bond traders would have bet on 5.50% or even higher.

On October 14th, the 10-year Treasury yield surged after the CPI report, hitting 5.33% minutes after the release. A few days later, it was markedly lower at 5.03%. The 30-year yield fell by a similar amount. Bonds rallied into the teeth of the bad inflation data.

Mohamed El-Erian, ex CEO of PIMCO and renowned bond expert, asked the obvious question on X:

Why are US government bond yields falling despite hotter-than-expected CPI and PPI inflation prints?

He offered two valid rationalizations. In this article, we walk through his two AI-related explanations and add two of our own. Importantly, we emphasize one we think matters most: the bond market may be starting to price in the risk that the Fed is being pushed into a policy mistake.

Explanation One: A Flight To Quality Out Of Tech

El-Erian's first driver is a flight to quality "out of formerly high-flying tech stocks that are now coming under pressure."

  • Many semiconductor stocks have been under pressure. The SOX semiconductor index fell almost 20% between October 1 and the PPI release on the 15th.
  • The Nasdaq, with a large semiconductor weighting, fell in sympathy. Foreign markets, including the tech-heavy Korea's KOSPI and Japan's Nikkei, were also down sharply.
  • As we show below, healthcare (XLV), consumer staples (XLP) and other beaten-up value sectors have rallied since October 1, while technology (XLK) moved in the opposite direction. This rotation was primarily a flight to quality within the equity market, but El-Erian thinks it may have also sparked some bond buying.

Additionally, El-Erian notes there are "emerging pockets of credit stress in the most vulnerable segments." To his point, CoreWeave, a large data center provider, saw yields on its debt rise from 9% to 15%. Because investors are demanding such high yields for CoreWeave's debt and some of its competitors, there is a growing concern that CoreWeave might be the AI trade's canary in the coal mine.

Credit-related issues, such as those noted, often lead to a flight to quality from corporate bonds to US Treasuries.

Explanation Two: Is Tech Still A Growth Engine?

El-Erian's second driver carries broader macroeconomic implications. AI-related capital spending has been a primary engine of economic growth. If investors are less willing to fund the AI build-out, and if firms can't afford to fund it, does the economic growth outlook dim?

Saxo's Charu Chanana noted:

Investors are becoming less willing to finance AI infrastructure growth at any cost.

With 10-year yields above 5% and some AI-related credit spreads at junk bond levels, the cost of financing data centers has risen sharply. Less AI capex means less GDP growth, and lower expected growth argues for lower inflation, which results in lower long-term yields.

Explanation Three: Short Covering And Signs Of Significant Demand

Our first addition to El-Erian's list is short covering. The bond market entered October leaning heavily toward higher yields.

To wit, CFTC data showed asset managers added more than 100,000 contracts to their short 10-year Treasury futures exposure in the week ending September 22, one of the largest weekly additions since 2023, according to Bloomberg. Furthermore, open interest in 10-year futures rose in 13 of 14 sessions through late September, and in 5-year futures in 11 of 12 sessions. Those are consistent with new short positions being added as yields rose.

The 10- and 30-year Treasury auctions on October 7th and 8th appear to have foreshadowed the reversal. Many investors expected weak demand for the new supply of debt. They got the opposite. Per our Commentary Bond Auctions: You Never Hear About The Good Ones:

The 10-year note auction on Wednesday sold $39 billion at a 5.300% high yield. It stopped 1.7 basis points through the when-issued level, meaning it cleared much better than the market expected. Thursday's 30-year $22.5 billion bond auction was similar. The box plots below, courtesy of Exante Data, show how far outside normal both readings sit. The bid-to-cover measures the amount of dollars bid for every dollar sold. The 10-year came in at 2.77 compared to a twelve-month average of 2.51, higher than any of the last 50 auctions. The 30-year was 2.54 against a 2.40 median, at the upper edge of the last 50 auctions.

Primary dealer participation may be the most important auction statistic. The Treasury's primary dealers must bid and absorb whatever nobody else wants. When an auction has a high percentage dealer take, it means the auction struggled, and Wall Street got stuck with inventory. Dealers took a mere 2.5% of the 10-year, their lowest share on record for the tenor, and 6.8% of the 30-year. Indirect bidders, largely foreign central banks and domestic institutions, took 80.3% and 72.3%, both far above their averages.

When dealers are left buying little at Treasury auctions, as we saw, it means real money buyers are absorbing supply at these yields. While the bond market didn't rally on the strong auctions, it certainly put short sellers on notice that demand was robust at yields above 5%. The rising demand may have prompted Treasury-bond buying to cover short positions. Given how offside the market was, the buying created a circular effect, forcing more short sellers to cover.

Explanation Four: The Bond Market Smells A Policy Mistake

The bond market may be beginning to believe that this month's hot inflation data will force the Fed's hand toward more, not fewer, rate hikes, ultimately resulting in a policy error.

The yield curve's changing shape over the past two weeks supports our view. The 2yr-10yr yield curve was 57 basis points on October 7th. Following the CPI and PPI reports, it flattened to 32 basis points. That's a relatively large 25-basis-point decline in two weeks, with most of it occurring on the days of the inflation data.

When all yields decline, but long-end yields fall more than short-term yields, that is called a bull flattener. A market that expects the Fed to tighten into a weakening economy buys long bonds and flattens the curve. A market fearing runaway inflation should result in a bear steepener reaction.

The front end of the yield curve prices the odds of Fed rate hikes. The long end is pricing the consequences.

Reasons To Fret A Policy Mistake

There are a few reasons we think the bond market should worry about the Fed.

First, the recent increase in inflation is largely a supply shock. Gasoline and diesel prices are rising because of the conflict with Iran, not because consumers are overheating. The Fed can't produce oil, but it can reduce demand for everything else.

Second, the labor market is weak. September payrolls rose just 29,000 and prior months were revised down by 60,000. Furthermore, the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2% and real earnings are flat to slightly negative, leaving little evidence of an inflationary wage-price spiral.

Third, consumers are being squeezed. The most recent retail sales beat estimates at 0.8%, but gasoline sales drove most of the gain. To wit, the Control Group, which the BEA uses in its GDP calculation, rose only 0.1. Essentially, higher gas prices are crowding out other spending.

Fourth, Fed policy is already restrictive by the Fed's own math. The September rate hike raised Fed Funds to 3.75% to 4.00%, above the Fed's own estimate of the longer-run neutral rate at 3.20%. The median dot plots in the latest Fed Economic Projections (SEP), along with commentary from some Fed members, suggest another rate hike or two is quite possible.

Lastly, financial conditions are tightening. The 10-year yield above 5%, 30-year mortgage rates near 7.50%, an 18-month high in the dollar, and widening credit spreads are all doing the Fed's work. Fed Funds rate hikes make financial conditions even more restrictive.

The Hawks Case

To be fair, Fed hawks have a rational case for raising rates further. The recent CPI report showed broader price increases across many goods and services, core PCE running near 3%, and, probably more importantly, inflation has been above the Fed's target for more than five years. The Fed is rightly concerned about inflation expectations becoming unanchored.

But the bond market is not voting on whether inflation is too high or what it has been. It is voting on where inflation will be and whether the Fed's inflation cure will not only heal the patient of its inflation problem but bring on recessionary side effects.

Summary

Falling bond yields amid hot inflation data are not a paradox. They reflect a flight to quality out of tech, doubts about AI as a growth engine, the unwinding of crowded short positions, and strong demand.

Most importantly, in our view, they signal concern that the Fed is responding to an energy-driven inflation shock and that inflation has been too high for too long, tightening into a slowing economy. The shape of the yield curve and the direction of long-end yields offer a good roadmap for what may happen next.

title: China 'Already Preparing' Trilateral Summit With US & Russia, Likely For November: Kremlin
desc:
China 'Already Preparing' Trilateral Summit With US & Russia, Likely For November: Kremlin

There's lots of talk of big trilateral meetings in the middle of this week, as some major parallel diplomacy is currently happening in St. Petersburg.

President Vladimir Putin's meeting with US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff has wrapped up, but already China is also in the house. Significantly, Chinese Premier Li Qiang is second-highest-ranking official in the country's Communist Party (CCP) hierarchy, under President Xi Jinping. He's meeting with Putin just after the Witkoff summit

Footage from St. Petersburg's Constantine Palace, where Putin is receiving Chinese Premier Li Qiang. Earlier today, the Russian president met Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, at the very same location. https://t.co/lUcKxvBMl9

— Brian McDonald (@BrianMcDonaldIE) October 21, 2026

Putin aide Yury Ushakov has in comments to reporters revealed that China has already begun preparing a trilateral meeting among the leaders of Russia, the US and China.

He indicated that could happen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen "if circumstances are favorable." This would be in just under a month, scheduled for November 17-18, 2026.

Ushakov said: "Our Chinese friends, who are hosting the APEC summit, will deal or rather are already dealing with its [the trilateral meeting] preparation. And if circumstances are favourable, they, our Chinese friends, will of course include this meeting in the program of events in Shenzhen."

Some further details laid out in Ushakov's briefing, via Bloomberg:

  • Potential meeting has been worked on at expert level, Ushakov says
  • Meeting would require all three leaders to be in same place at same time
  • Experts have outlined key topics for potential trilateral meeting at APEC summit
  • A single meeting between Putin, Trump and Xi wouldn't be enough to resolve war in Ukraine, Ushakov says.

One journalist and pundit described of Wednesday's remarkable events in Russia's second-largest city:

There’s an extraordinary diplomatic coincidence in St. Petersburg today. Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff is arriving to discuss peace in Ukraine, just as Chinese Premier Li Qiang, second only to Xi Jinping in Beijing’s political hierarchy, visits the city.

Peter the Great built St. Petersburg as Russia’s window onto the rest of Europe. Three centuries later, it will see Russia, America and China can discuss Europe’s affairs without troubling the EU.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang has arrived in St. Petersburg, where he was welcomed by Russian PM Mikhail Mishustin, ahead of tomorrow’s 31st regular meeting of the heads of government of Russia and China. Officials are expected to discuss bilateral trade, energy, industrial cooperation, agriculture and transport infrastructure, with several agreements due to be signed.

— Brian McDonald (@BrianMcDonaldIE) October 20, 2026

Ukraine's Zelensky has meanwhile tried to insist that his country's fate cannot be determined without him or Ukrainian representatives at the table.

On this, Trump said earlier this week: "I'm supporting stopping the war between Russia and Ukraine... Frankly, Zelensky is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it. I want to see people not die."

President Trump has meanwhile suggested that any future trilateral meeting would also focus on nuclear proliferation issues. Secretary of State Rubio has further hinted at this...

SECRETARY RUBIO: People need to grow up when it comes to foreign policy a little bit. I don't think it's unusual for the three most powerful, nuclear-armed nations on Earth to have their leaders communicate with each other. https://t.co/M4MhQCARnJ

— Department of State (@StateDept) October 20, 2026

We detailed Sunday that Putin reportedly first floated the idea of a trilateral meeting in an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump. That conversation also produced a deal for the US to buy Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale on the global market. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions were taking place over a potential meeting.

A potential three-way dialogue on Chinese soil would mark a big step for Xi in his efforts to elevate China’s role as a diplomatic power broker, said analysts who study China. Russian officials proposed the idea to Beijing through diplomatic channels and the Chinese side has indicated it wouldn’t object if Trump is on board.

Russian media captures some of Wednesday's high level dialogue:

'We see unilateral approaches and hegemony. Against this backdrop, Russia and China maintain close ties — a very important stabilizing factor' — Chinese Premier Li Qiang 'China is ready to work with Russia to deepen mutual respect and expand mutually beneficial cooperation' https://t.co/mbiJGh9c2j

— RT Intl (@RT_on_X) October 21, 2026

In the wake of prior late Sunday reports, Trump declared that he is indeed open to participating in a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin (but without Zelensky's involvement). Trump also offered that could be focused on denuclearization.

"I would do it" - Trump stated multiple times in Monday comments, stipulating that he'd like to see it happen if President Xi were on board, and saying it would likely be in China (since Xi just recently visited the US).

title: Clinton-Nominated Judge Says DOGE Illegally Accessed Data On Government Workers
desc:
Clinton-Nominated Judge Says DOGE Illegally Accessed Data On Government Workers

Authored by Zachary Stieber via The Epoch Times,

A federal judge ruled on Oct. 20 that a department aimed at making the government more efficient should not have been granted access to sensitive federal employee data.

Granting Department of Governmental Efficiency (DOGE) personnel access to government employee data contained in Office of Personnel Management systems violated the Privacy Act, which bars certain record disclosures and requires safeguards when disclosing other records, U.S. District Judge Denise Cote said in a 39-page ruling that granted plaintiffs final judgment.

"The defendants barely defend its legality, relying instead on what has happened since to argue that the case is moot and that prospective relief is unnecessary," wrote Cote, a judge for the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

Department of Justice lawyers had argued in court filings that DOGE agents needed access to the records as part of an effort to modernize government systems. The government did not explain why the modernization efforts required access to the sensitive records containing personally identifiable information, according to Cote.

Lawyers had also said that the agents were granted access in case they needed the data later, but the government has never linked the access to any of the agents' duties, the ruling stated.

The Department of Justice did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

President Donald Trump established DOGE shortly after taking office in 2025, and DOGE employees worked with various agencies to streamline operations.

Cote in June 2025 entered a preliminary injunction blocking the department from accessing federal employee records as the case proceeded, finding violations of the Privacy Act.

Professional groups, including the Association of Administrative Law Judges, brought the case and said DOGE's disclosure of employee personal data was illegal.

Twenty DOGE employees received access to Office of Personnel Management (OPM) systems from Jan. 20, 2025, to March 6, 2025, according to court documents. Some worked for OPM, but others received paychecks from other agencies.

Certain DOGE personnel had access to the systems through September 2025.

Only one of the agents remains at the office, according to the government, and he does not have access to systems containing personal employee data. DOGE itself shut down in July 2026.

The Office of Personnel Management has updated its disclosure policies, including specifying that only office employees and contractors, not detailees, can access those systems.

Cote said the updates were admirable but seemed to track with deadlines in the litigation. She also said the case was about misconduct stemming from "the failure of particular individuals," not deficient procedures.

Cote said it's unclear whether any relief is necessary at this juncture, given the developments surrounding DOGE and the office. She said she would be asking the parties to offer views on what relief, if any, is appropriate.

"In the meantime, the parties are encouraged to confer and explore whether they can reach an agreement on an appropriate resolution," she said.

title: Undercover Video Throws El-Sayed's Senate Campaign Into Chaos
desc:
Undercover Video Throws El-Sayed's Senate Campaign Into Chaos

Authored by Matt Margolis via PJ Media,

Abdul El-Sayed's Senate campaign is in full-blown panic mode after an undercover O'Keefe Media Group video caught one of its field organizers claiming the candidate takes overseas donations.

The video dropped on Monday. By the end of the day, the Michigan Democrat Party had confirmed that the organizer who spilled the beans about the campaign's illegal donations, Abdoul Beckwith, has been fired. No investigation, no review, no waiting to see how the story played out. Party officials cut him loose almost immediately, and the El-Sayed campaign rushed out a statement calling his comments "untrue," "wildly misinformed," and "not reflective of the campaign" while insisting it fully complies with Federal Election Commission rules.

Right. Sure. They would say that, wouldn't they?

So, what did Beckwith say?

Talking with an undercover journalist who posed as a volunteer at the campaign's Detroit operation, he dropped a true bombshell. El-Sayed "has people from overseas that donate to him," Beckwith said. Asked whether that was allowed, he acknowledged it wasn't.

He then described how the money supposedly moves, with family members or other intermediaries acting as conduits. "Everybody does it," Beckwith said.

But that isn't even the worst thing Beckwith revealed. When the undercover journalist raised the subject of Hamas, he explained why El-Sayed has to tread carefully around terrorist groups.

"He can't just say, you know, 'No, I don't support Hamas, you know, I reject all of them,' because he's going to lose the people that brought him up in the first place," Beckwith said. He made a similar point about the Muslim Brotherhood and worried that white and Jewish advisers could sway El-Sayed or "hijack" his positions.

BREAKING NEWS: Abdul El-Sayed Campaign Official Reveals El-Sayed Receives Overseas Donations, Admits Foreign Contributions Are Illegal Under Federal Law, Warns Denouncing Hamas Could Cost Support "You know, he [Abdul El-Sayed] has people from overseas that donate to him...No it is not allowed." "He [Abdul El Sayed] can't just say, you know, no, I don't support Hamas, you know, I reject all of them, because he's going to lose the people that brought him up in the first place." @AbdulElSayed @MikeRogersForMI

— James O'Keefe (@JamesOKeefeIII) October 19, 2026

Have you noticed this is a common theme among Democrat campaigns? Radicals at heart, they get nominated by primary voters and then spend the general election campaign trying to convince the broader electorate they aren't who they really are.

Now the El-Sayed campaign is struggling to clean up this mess. And believe me, the panic has spread beyond the campaign itself. Left-wing influencer Brian Krassenstein immediately rushed to run cover.

"This is the biggest nothing burger in the history of nothing burgers," Krassenstein claimed in a post on X.

If it's nothing, why did they fire Beckwith?

Krassenstein kept going. "Some random field organizer says that Abdul Al-Sayed is getting money from overseas," he wrote, adding, "First of all a field organizer has no inside knowledge of a campaigns finances, meaning his likely making it up, nor is getting money from overseas illegal if they are American citizens."

Why would Beckwith make it up? He thought he was chatting with a fellow volunteer, not a reporter, and he had no reason to invent a scheme that could sink his own candidate. Notice, too, how Krassenstein hedges. If he truly believed El-Sayed takes no overseas money, why bother arguing that overseas money from Americans is perfectly fine? People build fallback positions when they suspect the first defense won't hold.

The El-Sayed campaign now has a huge problem on its hands, and it knows it. The campaign could end this by opening its donor records to an independent audit. It won't do that.

title: Iran Attacks At Least Two More Tankers In Gulf Waters In Past 24 Hours
desc:
Iran Attacks At Least Two More Tankers In Gulf Waters In Past 24 Hours

There have been at least two more tanker attack incidents in Gulf waters and the Strait of Hormuz area over the last 24 hours.

First, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) says it received a delayed report of a projectile hitting a tanker off Iraq's coast, which occurred Tuesday. The tanker was struck reportedly thirty nautical miles off the coast of Al Faw, but the information has only emerged Wednesday. All crew members are said to be safe after the attack.

And on Wednesday another ship was hit "by an unknown projectile" off the coast of Oman, close to the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in a fire.

A fresh UKMTO report indicated the tanker is 11 nautical miles off the town of Bukha. The vessel is deemed "now at anchor" and all crew are safe and account for, with no reports of environmental impact.

Iranian state media is also reporting the latest attack. Tehran seeks for these assaults, which have been coming at record pace for the month of October, to be made as public as possible. It hopes to squeeze the Trump administration politically, imposing an economic cost on Americans, headed into the November midterm elections.

In the midst of all of this The Wall Street Journal, citing Kpler, has issued some surprising conclusions on Wednesday:

Persian Gulf oil exports have surpassed prewar levels, as an improvised shipping system under U.S. protection is helping tankers move oil through one of Iran’s fiercest waves of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

Middle East oil flows, including shipments through Hormuz and alternative routes across the region, averaged more than 24 million barrels a day in the week through Oct. 18, surpassing prewar levels of 23.3 million, according to ship tracker Kpler.

Preliminary figures show Hormuz oil flows, including offshore transfers in the Gulf of Oman, came to around 14 million barrels a day on average for the same period, or 82% of prewar levels.

Still, the same report also emphasizes that "Thinning global inventories leave little margin for error. The operation is also expensive, costs that ultimately flow through to consumers at the pump.

As for stalled negotiation efforts, Iranian media reports that Tehran informed Pakistan’s Army Chief Asim Munir on Tuesday that Tehran's conditions stand firm, and that talks won't materialize until these demands are met.

There are fears all-out war could resume after the November midterm elections in the US:

The current situation reminds me immensely of the days before February 28. Intense talks were underway, mediated by Oman. Today, Qatar is playing that role. But just like in February, it seems to me that Trump has already made up his mind and that the ongoing diplomacy is just for show. Just like in February, it is a devastating miscalculation.

— Trita Parsi (@tparsi) October 21, 2026

Washington wants a focus of these talks to be the nuclear file, while Iran has not budged in its insistence that this is not on the table. Iran's leaders have consistently said that the nuclear issue can only be dealt with after there is a permanent peace deal.

title: Undocumented Student Enrollment In California Schools Takes A Nosedive
desc:
Undocumented Student Enrollment In California Schools Takes A Nosedive

Authored by Bryan Hyde via American Greatness,

New immigrant and undocumented student enrollment has dropped sharply in California schools and public universities, driven by decreased border crossings and increased federal immigration enforcement.

Breitbart reports that the major drop in the number of kids of illegal migrants enrolled in California's schools is saving the state millions in education budget dollars.

The number of "newcomer" students born outside the U.S. who have been enrolled for 3 years or fewer has dropped from a record high of 236,958 in 2024-25 to 228,780 in 2025-26, with further declines anticipated.

New immigrant student enrollment has taken a nosedive in California schools

LEARN MORE: https://t.co/29ibPJbPxl https://t.co/xKCx0NhcJV

— EdSource (@EdSource) October 19, 2026

From 2017 to 2024, the Oakland Unified School District took in an average of 1,300 extra so-called "newcomer" students each year.

However, in 2025 the district only saw 498 "newcomers" enter the schools, and this year that number fell to 212, forcing the district to close almost two-thirds of its newcomer programs, according to EdSource.

L.A. schools recorded a drop of 46.5 percent in "newcomer" students, and San Juan Unified lost 13.6 percent of their "newcomer" students.

The decline has also impacted higher education within the University of California system as undocumented student enrollment backed by state financial aid dropped by 51 percent, falling from 1,181 to 579 students, according to Georgetown University.

California State University reports undocumented student enrollment receiving state aid fell by 48 percent, dropping from 2,219 to 1,148 students, influenced by restrictions on DACA and labor market exclusions.

Lower rates of cross-border migration have directly reduced the pipeline of newly arriving school-age children and the amount of education dollars directed at "newcomers" will necessarily see huge cuts in funding over the next few years.

Due to declining enrollment numbers, the infrastructure and administrators for these programs will also become unnecessary and the taxpayers will not have to direct as much money into school budgets.

Sam Finn, executive director of the California Newcomer Network told EdSource, "We're about to reach a cliff where we'll have had a couple years without significant entries."

Other contributing factors to the decline include federal policy changes and heightened immigration operations which have led families to avoid public spaces or relocate, compounding pre-existing statewide trends like falling birth rates and high housing costs.

title: Federal Agents Arrest 131 People With Alleged Gang Ties
desc:
Federal Agents Arrest 131 People With Alleged Gang Ties

Authored by Kimberly Hayek via The Epoch Times,

More than 100 gang members were arrested in less than a week, including members of MS-13 and Tren de Aragua, federal officials announced on Monday.

From Oct. 4 to Oct. 10, agents took 131 alleged gang-affiliated individuals into custody, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Of those, 22 were associated with MS-13 affiliates, and 13 were tied to Tren de Aragua, the department said.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) made 129 of the arrests, while Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) handled the remaining two.

"The best that America has to offer are on the frontlines every day to ensure that the worst of humanity cannot threaten or harm innocent Americans," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement about the gang member arrests.

"Under President Trump's leadership, we are smashing the gangs and cartels, making it impossible for them to do business in America, and removing their members from our country. Arresting and deporting illegal aliens, especially gang members, is how we make America safe again."

Among those arrested is Gustavo Adolfo Flores-Ramirez, an alleged MS-13 member from El Salvador. Flores-Ramirez is wanted in El Salvador for aggravated homicide, aggravated femicide, rape of a minor or incapacitated person, illegal handling of firearms, illicit grouping, and crimes involving public peace. He was arrested by ICE in Las Vegas on Oct. 14. Flores-Ramirez had been arrested by Border Patrol in 2021, deported to Mexico, and then re-entered illegally.

Jose Luis Perez-Arrias, an alleged Venezuelan Tren de Aragua member described as a suspected hitman, was arrested in Tallahassee, Florida, on Oct. 14. He entered through Texas in October 2023, and the Biden administration released him, according to DHS.

Emerson Jossiel Calderon-Hernandez, an alleged MS-13 member from El Salvador, was taken into custody in Washington on Oct. 13. His criminal history includes a conviction for second-degree assault and arrests for attempted first-degree murder, attempted second-degree murder, armed robbery, first-degree assault, reckless endangerment, and false imprisonment, DHS said. He entered through Texas in August 2012 and was released under the Obama administration.

On Oct. 13, agents in Denver arrested a 14-year-old Venezuelan associated with Los Piratas, a Tren de Aragua faction. He unlawfully possessed a Glock 48 pistol and faces charges of first-degree murder, criminal attempt with extreme indifference, first-degree assault with extreme indifference, first-degree kidnapping, aggravated criminal extortion, illegal discharge of a weapon, and conspiracy, according to DHS.

Gang Arrest Totals

Since Jan. 20, 2025, ICE has arrested 1,965 MS-13 affiliates and 1,553 Tren de Aragua affiliates.

In June, DHS said ICE had arrested more than 10,000 gang members so far during President Donald Trump's second term.

"These 10,000 criminals committed heinous crimes, including murder, assault with a deadly weapon, drug trafficking, racketeering conspiracy, robbery, and extortion," DHS stated.

title: China Imposes Export Curbs On Drones, Heavy Machinery
desc:
China Imposes Export Curbs On Drones, Heavy Machinery

Authored by Dorothy Li via The Epoch Times,

China said on Monday it would expand curbs on drone exports and restrict the sales of some heavy machinery to "sensitive countries" with which the communist regime has disputes.

Exporters will need a license to ship certain types of drones, such as those capable of traveling more than 300 km (186 miles) or flying beyond the natural line of sight, China's Ministry of Commerce said in an Oct. 19 statement, citing national security grounds. The drones' engines, operating systems, and technologies used for manufacturing will also be subjected to controls.

Other affected products include some tunnel-boring machines, walking excavators, and high-altitude concrete-spraying machines - all sophisticated machinery for building railway and road tunnels through mountains, according to a separate press release.

Decades of investment have helped China become the world's major supplier of tunnel-boring machines. Chinese media have long touted that the country makes 70 percent of such machines around the globe. Among the leading manufacturers are state-owned China Railway Engineering Equipment Group, whose website said its machines are delivered to overseas projects in 36 countries, including Italy, Australia, and Peru.

Separately, the regime's commerce ministry announced export restrictions on key components of dredgers, including heavy-duty pumps used to scoop up mud and sand from the seabed.

Overseas companies and individuals will be barred from transferring China-sourced dredger-related items to "sensitive countries and regions that have disputes with China," the ministry said.

Beijing didn't name any specific country. But some analysts, including Brookings Institution fellow Kyle Chan, said India could be a likely focus. The two neighbors have longstanding border disputes that escalated into war in the 1960s.

China has invested heavily in developing its dredger industry, with state-owned CCCC Dredging being the country's leading producer and contractor.

All three new export restrictions will be enforced beginning Nov. 18.

A ministry spokesperson said these newly added products have "clear dual-use characteristics," meaning they can be used for both military and civilian purposes. Chinese officials had already notified trading partners through export-control dialogue mechanisms ahead of the announcement, the spokesperson added.

The ministry also signaled tightened checks on dual-use products. Customs officers will detain goods and question export operators if they suspect a shipment includes controlled items. Exporters will have seven working days to respond and submit required documents such as contracts and receipts. The rules take effect immediately and also apply to cross-border e-commerce, mail, and travelers' luggage.

The expanded export controls came amid global concerns over reliance on China for raw materials and industrial products.

China restricted shipment of rare earths - a sector in which it accounts for about 70 percent of global supply - in late 2025 ahead of trade negotiations with the United States, and again earlier this year amid tensions with Japan. The sweeping restrictions have prompted the United States and other major economies to diversify the source of the supply chain critical for products ranging from smartphones and medical imaging to military equipment.

Last week, the commerce ministry unveiled sweeping export controls on dozens of technologies related to artificial intelligence as Beijing tightens controls on the strategic industry amid rivalry with the United States. Also added to the export-control list were biotechnology and technologies used to make solar equipment.

Senior U.S. and Chinese officials are set to hold a talk by November under a mechanism established at a September summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington.

Stablecoins moved more than $400 million an hour in adjusted transfer volume during the third quarter of 2026, as quarterly activity reached $891 billion, more than quadrupling since early 2023, according to a new report commissioned by Coinbase.

The report found that 73% of screened stablecoin transfer volume occurred outside US banking hours, including nights, weekends and holidays.

Distribution of stablecoin transfer volume by time of day. Source: Coinbase and The Block Research, via Dune Analytics

Seven of the 10 largest US banks have tested stablecoins or tokenized deposits for settlement, while 30% of mid-market companies conducting cross-border business are using or piloting stablecoins, up from 10% in 2024. Business-to-business payment volume also rose 36% year over year.

Conducted by The Block Research, the findings identified 293 million blockchain addresses holding stablecoins, exceeding the combined number of cards issued by American Express and Discover, though researchers cautioned that addresses do not necessarily represent individual users.

The report also estimated that moving 80% of international transactions onto stablecoin networks could add $155 billion to global GDP annually and free up roughly $3 trillion in liquidity currently held by banks to support cross-border payments.

Those projections are based on hypothetical adoption scenarios rather than observed economic gains. Researchers also acknowledged that widespread stablecoin adoption could reduce bank lending, potentially offsetting some of the benefits of faster and cheaper payments.

Survey finds growing demand for crypto services at US banks

A separate survey released Monday by the National Cryptocurrency Association found that 42% of US adults, representing approximately 112 million people, would be more likely to open an account with a bank offering crypto services or use that institution for more of their financial needs.

The survey found that 18% of US adults would like to buy or use stablecoins through their primary bank or financial institution. However, 64% said their bank, credit union or financial advisor had never raised the topic of cryptocurrency, while 43% did not know whether their bank offered crypto services.

Americans' interest in crypto banking services by demographic group.
Source: National Cryptocurrency Association, 2026 Crypto at the Bank Report

Stablecoin market cap remains flat despite rising transaction volumes

Despite increasing transaction activity, the stablecoin market capitalization stood at $301.42 billion on Tuesday, a decline of about 0.6% from $303.14 billion on Oct. 20, 2025, according to DefiLlama data.

Last week, Standard Chartered pushed back its forecast for the stablecoin market to reach $2 trillion from 2028 to 2030, citing slower supply growth. Citi, meanwhile, has projected a $1.9 trillion market by 2030 in its base case, with a bullish scenario reaching $4 trillion.

title: WNBA Officially Rejects Enes Freedom And Royce White For Being Men
desc:
WNBA Officially Rejects Enes Freedom And Royce White For Being Men

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told House Republicans in a letter last week that Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White cannot play in the league because they are men. Her letter did not include the definition of "women" that lawmakers had requested.

"With respect to your questions regarding eligibility, only women are eligible to play in the WNBA and the individuals you cite in your letter are both men," Engelbert wrote.

The America First Policy Institute, which represents Freedom, provided the letter to OutKick, which was released Tuesday.

BREAKING: The WNBA told Congress that Enes Freedom and Royce White are ineligible to play in the league because they are men and only women are eligible to play in the WNBA. pic.twitter.com/Oy2gABXQsZ

— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) October 20, 2026

Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) and four other House Republicans asked Engelbert about eligibility, player safety, and confrontations with fans after Freedom and White announced plans to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft while identifying as women. They asked how the league defines "women" under Article XIII, Section 1(a) of its 2026 collective bargaining agreement. That provision states, "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," but contains no definition of the term.

"The WNBA has just taken the first step in defining what a woman is for the sports community," Stutzman told Outkick. "By clearly labeling Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White as men, they have acknowledged that identifying as a woman does not change basic human biology."

Engelbert's letter announced no new eligibility rule, no broader policy on transgender athletes and no change to the bargaining agreement with the players' union.

Freedom called out Englebert for her hypocrisy.

"Cathy Engelbert cannot clearly define what a woman is, but she's absolutely certain that I'm a man," Freedom told OutKick. "I mean, how does that make sense? Who gets to decide? Who has the authority to determine whether someone is a woman?"

"So if the league is still working through these questions, how can its commissioner be so certain about my eligibility without explaining the standards that she's applying?" he said.

In August, the league's existing "anti-hate task force," made up of team presidents and general managers, discussed transgender participation and online abuse of players. The league said at the time that it faced no immediate eligibility issues and condemned the use of the subject to demean others.

"If the task force itself has not reached a clear definition, why is the commissioner making such a definitive statement?" Freedom asked.

Asked whether Engelbert had misgendered him, Freedom said, "Yes, 100%." He added, "I just want her to respect my identity because I am telling you that I identify as a woman."

Freedom said the goal of his bid is to push the league to limit play explicitly to biological females. "This is bigger than one basketball player," he said. "Who gets to determine someone's identity? The individual, the commissioner, the medical professional, or a committee or a task force?"

Enes Kanter Freedom called out the WNBA for declaring him "a man" and ruling him ineligible for the WNBA without clearly defining what a woman is. https://t.co/SoP6W1Y5oj

— Jackson Thompson (@JackThompsonFOX) October 20, 2026

"And who gets to determine eligibility to compete in women's category? So those may be different decisions, but the WNBA needs to explain where it draws the line," Freedom said.

The issue extends beyond Freedom and White. Julie Tetart, a French transgender basketball player who is biologically male, told OutKick in August of an interest in playing in the WNBA. "If they contact me, I won't say no. But you have to be realistic: I'm old, and there are far better players than me!" Tetart said.

The WNBA has not said what position it would take if Tetart sought to join the league.

The eligibility debate grew this summer after Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham voiced support for keeping transgender girls and women out of female sports. Her comments drew rallies during Fever road trips. Freedom has said Golden State Valkyries player Gabby Williams' support for transgender athletes inspired his effort.

Engelbert announced in September that she will retire at the end of 2026. Freedom said her successor could end his challenge with a single word added to the rules. "We are adding the word biological next to the word female, this whole thing will end the next day. I will walk to the sunset. They will not hear from me ever again," he said.

"I'm asking for consistency," Freedom said. "If they do not change the rules, they better select me in a WNBA draft in 2027."

"You cannot answer an eligibility question simply by declaring what somebody is," he said. "You need to explain the policy you are enforcing."

title: Ken Griffin Says AI Is "Almost Certainly" A Bubble As Corporate America Opens Its Anthropic And OpenAI Bills
desc:
Ken Griffin Says AI Is "Almost Certainly" A Bubble As Corporate America Opens Its Anthropic And OpenAI Bills

The man who runs one of the world's most profitable hedge funds and America's biggest market maker has a word for the AI trade, and it starts with a "b".

Speaking at the Future of Global Markets Conference in New York on Tuesday, Citadel founder Ken Griffin told Bloomberg that investors are "almost certainly" in the midst of an artificial intelligence bubble, as many companies are still figuring out how much they will spend on the technology and what, exactly, they are getting for it.

"Corporate America has been very uneven in its ability to extract value from its AI models. I think all of Corporate America is looking at their bills from Anthropic and OpenAI and going, 'Okay, we need to think about how to make sure we're getting productivity out of this.'"

That could be a problem because as BCA Research showed this week, so far AI has not produced an economy-wide acceleration in productivity growth. In fact, adjusted for shifts in utilization rates, total factor productivity growth was zero in Q2. Said otherwise, there has been zero productivity boost from AI!

And just in case anyone thought that was a throwaway line:

"Any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble. These bubbles, if we want to use that word, often coincide with these giant technological transformations."

In other words, the best-paid man in the room thinks the room is in a bubble, and he is fine saying so out loud. Which, for regular readers, will sound familiar: we have been warning since last October that the AI boom runs on debt, and lately the market has started doing the warning for us.

To be sure, nobody will care this is a bubble... until the market crashes, at which point everyone will scream how nobody warned them in advance. And just like that the new TBTF is born.

"Looking At Their Bills"

Griffin's timing was impeccable, maybe a little too impeccable. Hours earlier, the WSJ reviewed a fresh draft of Anthropic's S-1, which we broke down in "Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning." The short version: Anthropic booked $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of 2026, posted an $80.7 billion GAAP net loss (about $72 billion of which is a non-cash revaluation of financing instruments, leaving a still-hefty ~$8.7 billion underlying loss), and has signed more than $600 billion of mostly noncancelable compute contracts, with talks under way for another $150 billion. That would take the tab to as much as $750 billion.

Our reaction to the revenue headline was, well, brief:

*ANTHROPIC HAD $16.3B IN REVENUE IN FIRST HALF OF 2026: WSJ that's it?

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

Here is what that looks like on one chart: eventually someone has to pay for the blue bars, and Griffin just told us the customers are starting to check the invoices.

Griffin, for his part, said Anthropic's success will ultimately depend on proving to investors that its models are a must-have across every industry. That is a tall order when the price of the product keeps falling (and that ignores the fact that as "every industry" finds models are indispensably, it fires "almost every" worker currently employed, leading to a labor depression) . As we showed last week, Anthropic's token prices have tumbled to an all-time low:

Falling prices and decelerating growth are a tricky combination for a company with fixed, ten-year take-or-pay obligations. It is also why IPO investors marked the valuation down to $1.5 trillion last week after Anthropic's Q3 numbers showed the sequential growth rate hitting the brakes. Put differently, the bill keeps rising and the price per unit keeps falling, and the gap is what the IPO is supposed to fund.

From "Garbage" To "Depressed" To "Golden Era"

To be fair to Griffin, his AI views have had quite a year. Speaking in Davos in January, he called AI garbage, per Bloomberg. By May he told an audience at Stanford Business School that he was depressed by everything AI could achieve. On Tuesday he struck a sunnier tone, arguing the technology will unleash a wave of new business formation in the US:

"You're seeing the threat to white collar jobs playing out; as a business owner, you're seeing your competitive moats be filled in by bulldozers. At the same time, you're thinking that this will be a golden era for entrepreneurs."

Garbage, then depressing, then a golden era that happens to be a bubble. Three views in ten months is roughly how the market has traded AI too, so maybe he is just being consistent.

Griffin also pointed back to the days before the dot-com crash and some of the "fanciful" business models of that era:

"The companies that are on the other side of that bubble are the market leaders for decades to come. I just wish I'd kept my Amazon stock in that moment."

A fair point, with one footnote: anyone who kept their Amazon stock through that moment first had to sit through a drawdown of more than 90%. The winners on the other side of a bubble tend to get there the hard way.

Goldman: Breadth Is At Its Narrowest Since The Dot-Com Bubble

Griffin isn't the only one reaching for the 2000 analogy. Goldman's chief US equity strategist Ben Snider, in his latest US Weekly Kickstart (available to pro subs), notes that with the S&P 500 just 2% from its record high but the median S&P 500 stock 15% from its high, Goldman's preferred measure of breadth "remains near its narrowest level since the Dot-Com Bubble."

Snider also tackles the "productivity" question Griffin raised, from the earnings side. He expects S&P 500 EPS growth to slow from 29% in 2026 to 18% in 2027 (adjusting for accounting distortions), and warns that "slowing AI investment growth will be a fading tailwind." How big a tailwind? Goldman's Asia sales desk (Dani Wojdyla) puts it bluntly in this week's "Positioning Reset" note: "AI capex is currently contributing about half of S&P 500 EPS growth," an impulse Goldman expects "to diminish as capex growth slows and depreciation builds."

Translation: half of the earnings growth the market is paying for comes from companies spending money on AI, which shows up as someone else's revenue... and eventually as everyone's depreciation. The early Q3 read already shows the slope turning: 53% of S&P firms have beaten consensus EPS so far, above the 25-year average of 50% but well below the 64% rate of the past four quarters.

Last week Goldman's Tony Pasquariello argued breadth "isn't so bad"... then brought up the dot-com bubble twice, including a 2027 supply wildcard that could lift net US equity supply by the most since 2000. Anthropic's IPO, of course, is a big chunk of that wildcard.

Over at BofA, Michael Hartnett's team has done the bubble math on concentration. Peak concentration in the major bubbles of the past two centuries clustered around 40% (railroads were the outlier at 63%). The "AI Big 10" (Mag 7 plus Broadcom, AMD and Micron) recently hit 42%, above the 41% TMT peak in 2000:

Nothing says "healthy market" like a chart where the current reading sits between the Nifty Fifty and Japan in 1989.

Credit Got There First

If equity investors are only now discovering the word "bubble", the credit market has been pricing it for weeks. Per Goldman credit strategist Amanda Lynam's Global Credit Trader, "AI, Credit, and a Higher Cost of Capital" (also available to pro subs), USD HY AI-related spreads widened 25bp to 360bp over Treasuries, compared with just 2bp for non-AI issuers, with data center issuers leading the way:

Even Goldman's strategists, who just moved tactically overweight equities in their latest GOAL Kickstart, concede the point in the same note:

"Concerns on AI capex returns and funding are increasingly showing up in credit: CCC-BB spreads, hyperscaler CDS and neocloud OAS have all widened, with the latest move particularly sharp for neocloud issuers."

So Goldman is long the stocks and short the credit, while the credit is the one sending the warning. Their own Risk Appetite Indicator just "turned negative for the first time since March 2026," with all five sub-components down over the past month. Bullish, maybe... but not exactly confident.

The equity-credit gap is stark. As Goldman's basket desk showed in a chart we highlighted in "Trick Or Treat", hyperscaler equities were about 15% lower the last time hyperscaler credit spreads were this wide:

And the debt pile is only getting bigger. Goldman's credit team expects project finance plus direct hyperscaler issuance to hit $720 billion in 2027, up from $37 billion of project finance in all of 2025, with risks "firmly skewed to the upside":

The cracks are already showing where capital meets reality. Korea's Elice cratered 32% on its debut despite a retail tranche 400 times oversubscribed, and Australia's Nextdc imploded 45% and is mulling force majeure as protesters stall power to its Melbourne campus. Here is the updated casualty list:

Fink: The Bubble Can't Stop Inflating

Not everyone in the C-suite agrees with Griffin, or rather they agree, they just don't see any way out. Less than a day after the Citadel CEO's comments, BlackRock's Larry Fink took the opposite side, warning on Bloomberg TV from the Berlin Global Dialogue that the real danger is building too slowly. Per Bloomberg:

"If we don't build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost of compute is so high right now. And the faster we can build out more data centers, the more compute we have, the faster we can bring down the cost."

Incidentally, this is precisely the point we made a month ago:

The more data centers are lit, the faster this bubble pops

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) September 25, 2026

And, just to raise the stakes, Fink added that "If we slow down the build out of this technology, I think it really does jeopardize the economy." (Deutsche Bank's Christian Sewing, for what it's worth, also played down Griffin's bubble fears on Wednesday.)

Translation: the bubble is too important to stop inflating. Coming from the head of a firm whose infrastructure arm is among the biggest data center buyers on the planet, maybe that is not a huge surprise.

Fink does have a point on the physical bottleneck, and it is one we have been hammering for months: the constraint is power, permits and angry neighbors, which is why we keep arguing that "behind the meter" generation should be mandatory for new campuses. Nextdc's Melbourne fiasco is exactly that constraint in action, and so are the billions in Nvidia chips collecting dust in Amazon warehouses because there is nowhere to plug them in.

But the rest of his argument runs into the numbers above. If compute is so scarce and expensive, it is odd that Anthropic's token prices just hit an all-time low and its revenue growth is slowing (thank Chinese open-source models, which Dario is desperate to ban at the sovereign level). More importantly, building faster means borrowing faster, and Fink himself flagged the problem in the same interview:

"We're at a time now where we're finally unlocking private capital, and so the competition for capital is as large as I've ever seen in my professional career."

He also said bond yields are "flashing," adding: "Wake up, federal government. Our deficits are starting to have real large issues." Put the two together and you get the trade-off we have been describing for months: every extra dollar of AI debt is competing with Uncle Sam's ~$2 trillion deficit for the same duration buyers, with the 10Y already above 5%. As we noted on Sept 1, AI issuance has been crowding out Treasuries. In other words, Fink's cure for compute inflation (build more, faster, with borrowed money) is a fine recipe for bond-market inflation.

Who Holds The Bag On The Other Side?

Griffin's bubble call comes with a familiar bullish escape hatch: bubbles fund revolutions, and the survivors become the Amazons of the next two decades. That is probably right about the technology. It says very little about the price anyone pays to get there, or about who ends up holding the paper when the bills come due.

Griffin says it's a bubble; Fink says stopping it would be inflationary. Both can be right, which is precisely the problem. And right now the bills are piling up on both sides. On one side, Anthropic needs public investors to backstop as much as $750 billion of compute it has already promised to pay for. On the other, its biggest customers (per Griffin) are starting to ask what they are getting for their money. Meanwhile half of S&P earnings growth depends on the capex continuing, the credit market is already charging more to fund it, and the bond market (per Fink himself) is "flashing."

So we'll side with Griffin's first word over his last one. The AI buildout will probably produce a few generational winners, but the path from here to there looks a lot more like 2000-2002 than like a "golden era", and as usual, credit is telling equities which way the bubble deflates. If the man with the best seat in the house wishes he had kept his Amazon shares, maybe the more useful lesson is that he didn't buy more of them in March 2000.
